s1.title: Multiple choice — calculations and basic concepts

prim-add.title: Addition and subtraction
prim-add.subtitle: From small numbers to numbers up to 10,000
theory: We add and subtract place by place: first the ones, then the tens, then the hundreds, then the thousands.
Adding with regrouping: if the sum in one place is more than 9, carry one to the next place.
Subtracting with borrowing: if you don't have enough in one place, borrow 1 from the place to the left (it is worth 10 in your place).

prim-mul.title: Multiplication
prim-mul.subtitle: Times tables and multiplying bigger numbers
theory: Multiplication is repeated addition: 4 × 3 = 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12.
Bigger numbers: break them apart — 23 × 4 = 20×4 + 3×4 = 80 + 12 = 92.
The order of the factors doesn't change the result: a × b = b × a.

prim-div.title: Division (with remainder)
prim-div.subtitle: Dividing evenly and dividing with a remainder
theory: Division means splitting into equal parts: we find how many objects go in each group or how many equal groups we can make.
The relationship: Dividend = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder.
The remainder is always smaller than the divisor. You can never divide by 0.

prim-ord.title: Order of operations
prim-ord.subtitle: Parentheses, then × and ÷, then + and −
theory: The correct order: 1) parentheses ( ); 2) multiplication and division (left→right); 3) addition and subtraction (left→right).
2 + 3 × 4 = 2 + 12 = 14 (multiplication first).
(2 + 3) × 4 = 5 × 4 = 20 (parentheses first).

prim-nec.title: Find the unknown number
prim-nec.subtitle: Simple equations with one unknown
theory: You find the unknown number by using the inverse operation.
a × □ = b → □ = b ÷ a (a ≠ 0; we do not divide by 0). Always check your answer at the end.

prim-inmultire.title: Multiplication and division: properties and order of operations
prim-inmultire.subtitle: Factors, product, quotient and remainder, checking, parentheses, estimation, the unknown number
theory: The order of the factors does not change the product: 3 × 8 = 8 × 3 (3 rows of 8 or 8 rows of 3).
Grouping the factors does not change the product. Look for pairs that make 10, 100 or 1000: 2 × 5 = 10, 4 × 25 = 100, 8 × 125 = 1000.
Multiplication can be spread over a sum or a difference: 7 × 12 = 7 × 10 + 7 × 2. In reverse, the common factor is taken out: 6 × 23 + 6 × 7 = 6 × (23 + 7).
Any number multiplied by 0 gives 0; multiplied by 1 it stays the same. If a product is 0, at least one factor is 0.
Multiplying by 10, 100, 1000 adds one, two, three zeros at the end; dividing exactly by 10, 100, 1000 removes them: 47 × 100 = 4700, 5600 ÷ 100 = 56.
In columns you multiply starting with the ones; the tens of each product are carried to the next place. With a two-digit factor you multiply by the ones, then by the tens, and add.
Division answers two questions: “how many does each one get?” (sharing into equal parts) and “how many groups of … can be made?” (division by grouping).
Division is the inverse of multiplication: if 42 ÷ 6 = 7, then 7 × 6 = 42. Checking a division: quotient × divisor = dividend.
0 divided by any number (other than 0) gives 0; a number divided by 1 stays the same; a number divided by itself gives 1. We never divide by 0.
In long division you start with the largest place; what is left is brought down next to the next digit. If it cannot be divided, you write 0 in the quotient. At the end you check by multiplication.
Dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder, and the remainder is always less than the divisor.
Read the question carefully: “how many are completely filled?” asks for the quotient; “how many are needed so that everyone fits?” asks for the quotient plus 1 when the remainder is not 0.
A sum or a difference can be divided term by term: (40 + 8) ÷ 4 = 40 ÷ 4 + 8 ÷ 4 = 10 + 2.
Order of operations: first multiplications and divisions, then additions and subtractions. Operations of the same level are done from left to right.
What is inside the parentheses is calculated first: first the parentheses, then the square brackets, from the inside out.
The unknown factor = the product divided by the known factor. The unknown dividend = the quotient × the divisor. The unknown divisor = the dividend divided by the quotient.
Some equalities are true for any number (□ × 0 = 0), others for none (□ × 0 = 5). Think before you calculate.
Before calculating, estimate with rounded numbers: 39 + 48 ≈ 40 + 50 = 90. If your result is far from the estimate, check it.

prim-calcul-sistematic.title: Systematic calculation: with every number and the special cases
prim-calcul-sistematic.subtitle: Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division; 0 and 1; you cannot divide by 0
theory: Adding and subtracting 0: when you add or subtract 0, the number stays the same (7 + 0 = 7, 7 − 0 = 7). A number subtracted from itself gives 0 (7 − 7 = 0).
Crossing 10: in addition you first make 10 (8 + 5 = 8 + 2 + 3 = 10 + 3 = 13); in subtraction you first subtract down to 10 (13 − 5 = 13 − 3 − 2 = 10 − 2 = 8).

Multiplication is repeated addition: 6 × 3 means 6 groups of 3, that is 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 18. Any number multiplied by 0 gives 0, and multiplied by 1 it stays the same. The order of the factors does not change the product.
Division is the inverse of multiplication: 18 ÷ 3 = 6, because 6 × 3 = 18. Zero divided by a number different from 0 is 0; a number divided by 1 stays the same; a number divided by itself is 1.
You cannot divide by 0: 6 ÷ 0 makes no sense, because no number multiplied by 0 gives 6. Careful: 0 ÷ 6 is possible (it is 0), but 6 ÷ 0 is not possible.
Multiplying by 10, 100, 1000 adds one, two or three zeros at the end; exact division by 10, 100, 1000 removes the same number of zeros from the end.

prim-adunare.title: Addition and subtraction: properties and checking
prim-adunare.subtitle: Addends, regrouping, quick calculation, the unknown number
theory: Addition: addend + addend = sum. Subtraction: minuend − subtrahend = difference. “Increase by” means +, “decrease by” means −, and “how much greater” is found by subtraction.

In columns, you calculate place by place, starting with the ones. In addition, when a place goes over 9, you write the ones and carry 1 to the next place. In subtraction, when there is not enough, you borrow 1 from the next place (1 ten = 10 ones).
The order of the addends does not change the sum: 27 + 8 = 8 + 27. Start with the larger number — you count less.
Grouping the addends does not change the sum. Look for pairs that make round numbers: 37 + 25 + 63 = (37 + 63) + 25 = 100 + 25 = 125.
With zero: a + 0 = a, a − 0 = a, a − a = 0.
Addition is checked by subtraction: sum − one addend = the other addend. Subtraction is checked by addition: difference + subtrahend = minuend.

In subtraction the order matters: 42 − 17 is not the same as 17 − 42. Several subtractions in a row are done from left to right; subtracting two numbers one after the other means subtracting their sum.

If one addend increases by k, the sum increases by k. If the minuend increases by k, the difference increases by k; if the subtrahend increases by k, the difference decreases by k; if both increase by k, the difference stays the same.
The unknown addend = the sum − the known addend. The unknown minuend = the difference + the subtrahend. The unknown subtrahend = the minuend − the difference. At the end, check by substituting.

prim-aprof-operatii.title: Operations: special cases
prim-aprof-operatii.subtitle: 0 and 1, the check, the remainder, the order of operations, estimation
theory: Special cases in addition and subtraction: a + 0 = a, a − 0 = a, a − a = 0. The order of the addends does not change the sum, but in subtraction the order matters.
Special cases in multiplication and division: a × 0 = 0, a × 1 = a, a ÷ 1 = a; for a other than 0: 0 ÷ a = 0 and a ÷ a = 1. You can't divide by 0.

Division with remainder: dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder, and the remainder is less than the divisor. If the dividend is less than the divisor, the quotient is 0 and the remainder is the dividend itself. In problems, the remainder may call for one more boat or one more box.

Order of operations: first the round parentheses, then the square brackets; then multiplications and divisions, from left to right; last additions and subtractions. Estimation (rounding the numbers) quickly shows whether a result is plausible.

prim-num.title: Numbers: comparing, sequences, rounding
prim-num.subtitle: Natural numbers up to 1,000,000
theory: First we count the digits: the number with more digits is greater. If they have the same number of digits, we compare them digit by digit, starting with the highest place value.
Rounding to the nearest ten: look at the ones digit (≥5 → round up).
Rounding to the nearest hundred/thousand: look at the digit just to the right of the place you are rounding to.

prim-frac.title: Fractions
prim-frac.subtitle: Fraction of a number, adding, and comparing (fourth grade)
theory: A fraction a/b means a parts of a whole divided into b equal parts.
Fraction of a number: divide the number by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator.
With the same denominator: add the numerators and keep the denominator; the fraction with the bigger numerator is the bigger one.

prim-numere.title: Numbers: writing, order, sequences
prim-numere.subtitle: Tens and ones, the number line, even and odd, rounding, Roman numerals
theory: Natural numbers are written with the digits 0, 1, 2, …, 9. Step by step, we learn the numbers up to 100, then up to 1000, 10,000 and 1,000,000.

“How many?” asks how many objects there are; “which place?” asks for the position in a row — be careful which end you start counting from. Place from the right = how many there are − place from the left + 1.
10 ones make a ten, 10 tens make a hundred, 10 hundreds make a thousand. The value of a digit depends on its place: in 3482, the hundreds digit is 4, but the number contains 34 whole hundreds.
Zero holds the place of an empty position: 604 means 6 hundreds, no tens and 4 ones. A number with several digits does not start with 0.
The successor of n is n + 1, its predecessor is n − 1; 0 has no predecessor. Consecutive numbers differ by 1.
On the number line, numbers increase to the right. To read a point, start from the nearest written number and count the steps. Placing a number between two others: 50 < 57 < 60.
Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, and odd numbers in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. Even + even = even, odd + odd = even, even + odd = odd.
In a sequence, look for the rule: by how much each number goes up or down. In a repeating pattern, divide the place by the number of shapes in the group: the remainder shows the shape.
Rounding to the nearest ten: you look at the ones digit — 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 round down; 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 round up (43 ≈ 40, 47 ≈ 50). For hundreds you look at the tens, for thousands at the hundreds.

Roman numerals: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1000. A smaller numeral placed before a larger one is subtracted (IV = 4, IX = 9, XL = 40, XC = 90, CD = 400); placed after it, it is added (VI = 6, XI = 11).

prim-fractii.title: Fractions: parts of a whole
prim-fractii.subtitle: Half and quarter, fractions on the number line, equivalent fractions, addition and subtraction, hundredths
theory: A half: the whole divided into 2 equal parts. A quarter: the whole divided into 4 equal parts. Half of 18 means 18 ÷ 2 = 9.
The fraction 3/5: the denominator (5) shows how many equal parts we divided the whole into, the numerator (3) shows how many parts we take.

A fraction is less than one whole when the numerator is smaller than the denominator (3/5), equal to one whole when they are equal (5/5 = 1), and greater than one whole when the numerator is larger (7/5).
On the number line, divide the segment from 0 to 1 into as many equal steps as the denominator shows; 3/4 means 3 steps of one quarter each.
Equivalent fractions show the same part of the whole: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6. You get them by multiplying (or dividing) the numerator and the denominator by the same number.
With the same numerator, the fraction with the smaller denominator is greater: 1/3 > 1/5, because one third is a bigger piece than one fifth.
With the same denominator, you add the numerators, and the denominator stays the same: 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7.
With the same denominator, you subtract the numerators, and the denominator stays the same: 7/9 − 4/9 = 3/9.
A whole has as many parts as the denominator shows: 1 = 7/7. What is still needed to make the whole: 7/7 − 3/7 = 4/7.
If you know a part, first find a single piece, then the whole: 3/5 of the sum = 30 lei ⇒ 1/5 = 10 lei ⇒ the whole sum = 50 lei.
A square with 100 small squares: each small square is one hundredth (1/100). 3/10 = 30/100, and 50/100 = 1/2.

prim-aprof-numere.title: Numbers: special cases
prim-aprof-numere.subtitle: Zero, the number of digits, rounding that moves up to the next place, positions in a line
theory: Two numbers are compared first by the number of digits: the one with more digits is greater (1009 is greater than 999). With the same number of digits, you compare the digits from left to right.
The digit 0 holds the place of a missing place value: in 9009 there are no hundreds and no tens. A number contains more tens than the tens digit shows: 350 contains 35 tens.

When rounding, you look at the digit after the place you round to: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — you round down; 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 — you round up. Sometimes you move up to the next place: 96 rounded to the nearest ten is 100.
When you count positions in a line, don't forget the person being talked about: the ones in front, her, and the ones behind.

prim-aprof-fractii.title: Fractions: special cases
prim-aprof-fractii.subtitle: The whole, equal fractions, comparison, parts of a quantity
theory: A fraction whose numerator equals its denominator is a whole: 8/8 = 1. A fraction with numerator 0 means no part: 0/5 = 0. Halves, quarters and all the parts of a whole must be equal to each other.
When adding and subtracting fractions with the same denominator, you only add or subtract the numerators; the denominator stays the same: 1/5 + 2/5 = 3/5.
With the same denominator, the fraction with the greater numerator is greater. With the same numerator, the fraction with the smaller denominator is greater: 1/2 is greater than 1/10.
The whole from a part: if 2/3 of a road means 12 km, one third means 12 ÷ 2 = 6, and the whole road 6 × 3 = 18.

prim-mas.title: Units of measurement
prim-mas.subtitle: Length, mass, capacity, time, and money
theory: Length: 1 m = 100 cm = 1000 mm; 1 km = 1000 m.
Mass: 1 kg = 1000 g. Capacity: 1 l = 1000 ml.
Time: 1 hour = 60 minutes. Money: 1 leu = 100 bani.

The clock: the small hand shows the hour, and the big hand shows the minutes. When the big hand is on the 12, it is exactly on the hour. A week has 7 days: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.

prim-geo.title: Geometry: shapes, perimeter, area
prim-geo.subtitle: Geometric shapes, squares and rectangles
theory: Flat shapes: a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners; a rectangle has 4 right angles and equal opposite sides; a square has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles (a square is a rectangle with all sides equal); a circle has no corners.
Perimeter = the length of the outline. Square with side l: P = 4 × l. Rectangle with length L and width l: P = 2 × (L + l).
Area of a rectangle = L × l; area of a square = l × l.
Length is measured in units of length (cm, dm, m); area, in square units (cm², dm², m²). If the sides are in cm, the area comes out in cm².

prim-unit.title: Unit conversions
prim-unit.subtitle: Length, mass, capacity, time, and money — both ways
theory: Length: 1 km = 1000 m; 1 m = 10 dm = 100 cm = 1000 mm; 1 dm = 10 cm; 1 cm = 10 mm.
Mass: 1 t = 1000 kg; 1 kg = 1000 g. Capacity: 1 l = 10 dl = 100 cl = 1000 ml.
Time: 1 day = 24 hours; 1 hour = 60 minutes; 1 minute = 60 seconds; 1 week = 7 days; 1 year = 12 months.
Money: 1 leu = 100 bani.
From a larger unit to a smaller one, you multiply: 3 m = (3 × 100) cm = 300 cm. From a smaller unit to a larger one, you divide: 500 cm = (500 ÷ 100) m = 5 m.

prim-masurari.title: Measurement: length, mass, capacity, money, time
prim-masurari.subtitle: The ruler, unit conversions, change and budget, the clock, the calendar, durations
theory: When you measure, you count how many times the unit fits into the length. With a bigger unit you get a smaller number; that is why we use standard units, the same for everyone.
Length is measured with a ruler or a tape measure (cm, m, km), mass with a scale (g, kg, t), capacity with measuring jugs (ml, l), time with a clock.
On the ruler, a segment is measured from 0. If it does not start at 0, the length = where it ends − where it starts. 1 cm = 10 mm.
1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 km = 1000 m. When converting from big units to small ones you multiply; from small to big you divide.
When you add or subtract measurements written in two units (2 m 40 cm), first convert them to the same unit (240 cm).
Our currency is the leu; 1 leu = 100 bani. 3 lei and 50 bani = 350 bani.
Change = the amount given − the price. To know whether you have enough money, first work out how much everything you buy costs.
The small hand shows the hour, the big hand shows the minutes: at 12 = the hour exactly, at 3 = a quarter past (15 minutes), at 6 = half past (30 minutes), at 9 = 45 minutes. An hour has 60 minutes.
A week has 7 days, a year has 12 months and 365 days (a leap year has 366). April, June, September and November have 30 days each.
Duration = end time − start time. First count up to the next hour, then the whole hours, then the remaining minutes.
A decade = 10 years, a century = 100 years, a millennium = 1000 years. The years 2001–2100 form the twenty-first century.

prim-figuri.title: Shapes and solids: orientation, lines, perimeter, area, cubes
prim-figuri.subtitle: Positions and grids, segments and angles, square, rectangle, circle, symmetry, perimeters and areas, solids and nets
theory: Left, right, up, down, above, below, between: when you turn your back, left and right swap places.
On a grid, a box is found by its column (the numbers at the bottom) and its row (the numbers on the left, from bottom to top). Moving to the right changes the column, moving up changes the row.
A segment has two endpoints; a ray has one endpoint and goes on forever; a line has no endpoints. A broken line is made of segments placed end to end. Through two points passes exactly one line.
Parallel lines never meet (train tracks). Perpendicular lines meet forming right angles (the corner of a sheet of paper).
An angle has a vertex and two sides. A right angle is like the corner of a sheet of paper; an acute angle is smaller, an obtuse angle is larger than a right angle.
A polygon is a closed broken line: it has as many vertices as sides. A diagonal joins two vertices that are not adjacent; a triangle has no diagonals, a rectangle has 2.
A triangle has 3 sides and 3 vertices. Its perimeter = the sum of the sides. A triangle with all sides equal is equilateral.
A rectangle has 4 right angles; its opposite sides are equal and parallel. The longer side is the length, the shorter one is the width.
A square has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles. A square is a rectangle with all sides equal.
A parallelogram has opposite sides parallel and equal. A rhombus is a parallelogram with all sides equal. With right angles, a parallelogram becomes a rectangle, and a rhombus becomes a square.
A circle is the round line; all its points are at the same distance (the radius) from the center. The diameter = 2 radii. The inside of a circle, together with the circle, is the disk.
A figure is symmetrical if, folded along its line of symmetry, the two halves match exactly (like the wings of a butterfly). The right half is the mirror image of the left half.
Lines of symmetry: the square 4, the rectangle 2, the equilateral triangle 3, the circle countless; an ordinary parallelogram has none.
The perimeter is the length of the outline: the sum of all the sides. The fence of a garden is calculated with the perimeter.
The perimeter of a square: P = 4 × side. Side = P ÷ 4.
The perimeter of a rectangle: P = 2 × (L + l). Half of the perimeter is L + l.
On a grid, the perimeter is found by counting the sides of small squares along the outline. When you join two figures, the joined sides are no longer part of the outline.
Area is the size of a surface: how many squares with a side of 1 cm (1 cm²) cover the figure.
The area of a rectangle = L × l (rows of small squares); the area of a square = side × side.
A composite figure is split into rectangles and the areas are added; for a figure with a piece cut out, the area is subtracted. By cutting and moving the pieces, the area does not change.

The perimeter is a length (cm); the area measures a surface (cm²). Figures with the same perimeter can have different areas, and the other way around. When the side of a square doubles, the perimeter doubles, and the area becomes 4 times as large.

Solids: the cube (a die), the cuboid (a box), the sphere (a ball), the cylinder (a tin can), the cone (an ice cream cone), the pyramid. Flat shapes (square, circle) are drawn on paper; solids take up space.
A cube has 6 equal square faces, 12 equal edges and 8 vertices. A cuboid (rectangular box) has 6 rectangular faces, equal in pairs, 12 edges and 8 vertices.
A cylinder has 2 bases (circles); a cone has one base and a point; a sphere has no flat face; a pyramid has one base and triangular side faces. Solids with a curved surface can roll.
A net shows all the faces of a solid spread out on paper: a cube = 6 squares (for example in a cross), a cuboid = 6 rectangles, a cylinder = 2 circles and a rectangle.
The volume of a solid made of small cubes = how many cubes it contains: the cubes in one layer × the number of layers.

prim-aprof-masurari.title: Measurements, money and time: special cases
prim-aprof-masurari.subtitle: Units, conversions, change, clock and calendar
theory: In conversions, watch the zeros: 2 km and 8 m mean 2000 + 8 = 2008 (meters), and 3 kg and 40 g mean 3000 + 40 = 3040 (grams). Half a kilometer, half a kilogram or half a liter means 500 meters, grams or milliliters.
On a ruler, the length of a segment that doesn't start from 0 is the difference of the marks at the ends. A smaller unit of measure fits more times into the same length.
The change can be 0, when you pay the exact amount. If the price is greater than the money you have, the difference shows how much more you need.
15:00 is 3 p.m. (15 − 12 = 3). A duration that goes past midnight is calculated in two pieces: up to hour 24, and after it. The year 2000 is the last year of the twentieth century.

prim-aprof-figuri.title: Shapes and solids: special cases
prim-aprof-figuri.subtitle: Recognition, perimeter, area, symmetry, solids
theory: A segment has two endpoints, a ray has only one, and a line has none. Two parallel lines never meet. A polygon has as many vertices as sides; the circle is not a polygon.
Every square is a rectangle and a rhombus, but not every rectangle or rhombus is a square. If the length of a rectangle is equal to its width, the rectangle is a square.

The perimeter goes around the figure, the area covers it. When we glue two figures together, the glued sides are no longer part of the outline, so the perimeter is less than the sum of the perimeters. Figures with the same area can have different perimeters.

A point and its symmetric point are at the same distance from the line of symmetry, on opposite sides. The letter A has one line of symmetry, the letter H has two, and a rhombus that is not a square has two (its diagonals).
The cube and the cuboid each have 6 faces, 8 vertices and 12 edges. The cone has one vertex, and the pyramid with a square base has 5 vertices and 4 triangular faces.

prim-prob.title: Word problems
prim-prob.subtitle: Simple word problems (first grade) and word problems by method
theory: Bar model method: we draw bars/segments to see how the quantities are related.

Comparison method: we make the amount of one quantity the same in both situations, then subtract to get rid of that quantity. E.g.: a book and 2 pens cost 30 lei, and a book and 3 pens cost 34 lei ⇒ one pen costs 34 − 30 = 4 lei.
Unit method: first we find the value of a single unit.
Working backwards: we start from the result and do the inverse operations, in reverse order.

prim-metode.title: Word problems by method: bar model, comparison, working backwards, trials
prim-metode.subtitle: Choosing the operation, two-step problems, missing or useless information, the unit method
theory: Read the problem and choose the operation from the key words: “gets more”, “in total” — addition; “gives away”, “burst”, “how much more” — subtraction; “times as many”, equal groups — multiplication; “equally”, “times fewer” — division. Careful: ask yourself who has more. “Ana has 4 times as many as Mihai” and you are asked about Mihai ⇒ divide.
In two-step problems, first ask the intermediate question (what do you need to know first?), solve it, then answer the question of the problem.
Check the information: is something necessary missing? (then the problem cannot be solved); is something useless? (don't use it); does the question fit the information?
Bar model — sum and difference: draw two segments, the big one with the “extra” piece. Take the extra away from the sum, divide by 2 ⇒ the small number; add the difference ⇒ the large number.
Bar model — ratio: the small number = 1 segment, the large number = as many segments as the ratio says. The sum (or the difference) is divided by the number of segments ⇒ one segment.
The unit method: first find the value for a single unit (the price of one item, the weight of one piece, the distance for one hour), then multiply by the number asked for.
The comparison method: when two purchases have the same items of one kind, the difference in price comes only from the items that differ. From there you find the price of one, then of the other.
Working backwards: you start from the result and undo the operations from the last to the first, each with its inverse (+ ↔ −, × ↔ ÷). At the end, check by going forwards.
Organized trials: try in order (1, 2, 3… or the pairs with a given product), check each trial and stop at the one that meets all the conditions.

prim-date.title: Data and logic: tables, charts, true or false
prim-date.subtitle: Sorting by criteria, reading tables and charts, collecting data, simultaneous conditions
theory: Objects are grouped by a criterion (color, shape, even/odd, ones digit). An object that does not fit the criterion does not belong to the group.
In a table, the data are in rows and columns. The total of a row or a column is found by adding its numbers.
In a bar chart, a taller bar means more; the height is read on the axis with numbers. In a pictogram, each symbol is worth as much as the key says.
When you collect data, you count it, record it (for example with tally marks) and then interpret it: which value appears most often, how much it makes in total, how much is missing.
A mathematical statement is true or false — you check by calculating. When there are several conditions, a number must meet all of them at the same time.

prim-aprof-probleme.title: Problems and data: special cases
prim-aprof-probleme.subtitle: Solving methods, extra data, tables and charts
theory: The words in the text don't choose the operation on their own: “Dan has 25 marbles, 8 more than Radu” means that Radu has 25 − 8 = 17 marbles. First work out who has more.
Not all the data in a problem is needed, and sometimes a piece of data is missing and the problem can't be solved. Pick only the data that answers the question.

The drawing (bar model) method: you draw equal segments for the parts. If the difference of two numbers is 0, the numbers are equal. If one gives the other 2 and they end up equal, the difference between them was 4.
Working backwards: you start from the result and do the inverse operations, in reverse order. You check by redoing the path from the start.
In a table or a chart, the greatest value can appear more than once. A statement of the type “every…” is false if you find a single example that doesn't fit.

s1-ordinea.title: Order of operations
s1-ordinea.subtitle: Numerical calculations with parentheses and powers
theory: Order of operations: 1) parentheses and brackets ( ) [ ] { }; 2) powers and square roots; 3) multiplication and division (from left to right); 4) addition and subtraction (from left to right).
Example: 18 − 2 · 7 = 18 − 14 = 4 (multiplication first, then subtraction).

Watch out: follow the order — parentheses, powers, ×/÷, then +/−. Divisibility: a number is divisible by 9 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 9; the remainder when dividing by 9 is the same as the remainder of the sum of its digits divided by 9. The two-digit integers go from −99 to −10 and from 10 to 99. The digit-sum rule is for natural numbers.

s1-procente.title: Percents
s1-procente.subtitle: p% of a number, price increases, and discounts
theory: To find p% of a number N, calculate N · p/100.

Price increase of p%: N + N·p/100. Discount of p%: N − N·p/100. What percent of N the number a is: (a/N) · 100. After a p% discount, the new price is (100 − p)% of the original price, so the original price = new price · 100 ÷ (100 − p) (for p less than 100).

Watch out: p% of N = N·p/100 (not N − p). Ratios: from a/m = b/n = k we get a = m · k and b = n · k; in a proportion, the product of the extremes = the product of the means; the two quantities in a ratio are written in the same unit.

s1-reale.title: Real numbers: opposite, absolute value
s1-reale.subtitle: The opposite, the absolute value, and types of numbers
theory: The opposite of a number a is −a. A number plus its opposite is 0: a + (−a) = 0.
The absolute value |a| is the distance from 0: |6| = 6, |−6| = 6.
Rational numbers can be written as fractions a/b, where a and b are integers, b ≠ 0. Irrational numbers cannot be written this way: e.g., √2, π (decimals that never end and never repeat).

Watch out: the absolute value is always ≥ 0; the opposite changes the sign. The reciprocal of a (a ≠ 0) is 1/a. The interval (a, b] does not contain the endpoint a (round bracket), but it contains the endpoint b (square bracket). A ∩ B = the elements that the sets A and B have in common.

s1-fractii.title: Decimals ↔ fractions
s1-fractii.subtitle: Conversions, including repeating decimals
theory: Terminating decimal: 1.2 = 12/10 = 6/5 (simplify).
Simple repeating decimal: write the repeating part in the numerator and one 9 for each digit of the repeating part in the denominator. Example: 0.(5) = 5/9; 0.(12) = 12/99 = 4/33.

Similarly, 1.(4) = 1 + 0.(4) = 1 + 4/9 = 13/9. Mixed repeating decimal: in the numerator, the number written without the decimal point (with the repeating part once) minus the number formed by the digits before the repeating part; in the denominator, one 9 for each digit of the repeating part and one 0 for each non-repeating digit after the decimal point. Example: 0.8(3) = (83 − 8)/90 = 75/90 = 5/6.
Watch out: to get the decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator.

s1-proportii.title: Proportions and simple equations
s1-proportii.subtitle: Finding the unknown
theory: In a proportion a/b = c/d, we have a·d = b·c (product of the extremes = product of the means).
A first-degree (linear) equation: isolate the unknown by moving the terms and dividing by the coefficient. Example: 3x + 5 = 20 → 3x = 15 → x = 5.
Watch out: in a proportion, you cross-multiply; you don't add.

s1-date.title: Reading data and averages
s1-date.subtitle: Charts, the mean, the median
theory: The mean (average) = (sum of the values) ÷ (number of values).
The median = the middle value after you put the values in order; if there is an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values.
In a bar chart, the height of a bar shows the value.
Watch out: mean = sum ÷ number of values.

s1-elevi.title: Who is right? (square roots)
s1-elevi.subtitle: “Four students calculated…”: square roots, conjugates, powers
theory: Product of conjugates: (m + n√k)(m − n√k) = m² − n²·k (difference of squares), so the result no longer has a square root.
Taking factors out from under a square root: √18 = √(9 · 2) = 3√2; then combine only like radicals: 3√2 − √2 = 2√2.
Example: (6 + 2√5)(6 − 2√5) = 36 − 4 · 5 = 16, so the geometric mean of the two numbers is √16 = 4.
Watch out: (n√k)² = n² · k, not n · k; and the sign between the squares is a minus, not a plus (36 + 20 = 56 is the typical wrong answer).

s1-adevarat.title: True or false?
s1-adevarat.subtitle: Charts, practical reasoning, comparisons
theory: Check the statement with a quick calculation; if even one part doesn't match, the statement is false.
Bar chart: the height of a bar = how many students; “a score of at least 8” means the scores 8, 9, and 10.
Example: 3√5 = √45 and 2√11 = √44, so 3√5 > 2√11 (compare the numbers under the square roots).
Watch out: the interval [−2, 3] contains 6 integers (the endpoints count); a 10% price increase followed by a 10% price decrease does NOT bring back the original price.

s1-numere-calcule.title: Numbers, square roots, ratios and probability
s1-numere-calcule.subtitle: Numbers and calculations for grades V–VII
theory: A number is a perfect square if it is the square of a natural number: 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, …, 144, 169, 196, 225. The last digit of a perfect square cannot be 2, 3, 7 or 8.
Divisibility rules: by 2 — an even last digit; by 5 — last digit 0 or 5; by 10 — last digit 0; by 3 (by 9) — the sum of the digits is divisible by 3 (by 9).
The last digit of aⁿ repeats periodically: for 2: 2, 4, 8, 6; for 3: 3, 9, 7, 1; for 7: 7, 9, 3, 1; for 4 and 9 the period is 2.
√(a²) = |a|; √a · √b = √(a · b) and √a ÷ √b = √(a ÷ b), for a, b ≥ 0 (b ≠ 0 for division); to rationalize a ÷ √b, multiply the numerator and the denominator by √b.
Inversely proportional quantities have a constant product: if one becomes k times larger, the other becomes k times smaller. In a sequence of equal ratios a/x = b/y = c/z = k.
The scale 1:n means that 1 cm on the map stands for n cm in reality.
The probability of an event = number of favorable outcomes ÷ number of possible outcomes (equally likely outcomes); it is between 0 and 1.

s3-numere-pasi.title: Calculations step by step
s3-numere-pasi.subtitle: Seven chains; the last step is the whole problem
theory: Identify the data and the quantity asked for. Choose the right property: divisibility, the period of the last digit, the sum of consecutive numbers, square roots, proportionality, scale or probability.

Link each result to the next calculation. For the whole problem, start from the given data and keep only the steps you need; check the sign with square roots, the units and the lowest-terms form of the fractions.

s1-ecuatii-inecuatii.title: Integers, equations, inequalities and systems
s1-ecuatii-inecuatii.subtitle: Exercises for grades VI–VIII
theory: The sign rule: when multiplying and dividing, equal signs give a positive result, and different signs give a negative result.

To solve a first-degree equation, remove the parentheses, bring the terms with x to one side and the numbers to the other, then divide by the coefficient of x. Check the solution by substituting it into the equation.
|x| = a has the solutions x = a and x = −a if a > 0, the solution x = 0 if a = 0 and no solution if a < 0.
In an inequality, when you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, the inequality sign is reversed.

A system of two equations is solved by substitution (express one unknown from one equation and substitute it into the other) or by elimination (add or subtract the equations so that one unknown disappears).
x² = a has the solutions √a and −√a if a > 0, the solution x = 0 if a = 0, and no real solution if a < 0; a product is 0 if at least one factor is 0: (x − 2)(x + 3) = 0 ⟹ x = 2 or x = −3.

s1-fractii-operatii.title: Fractions: comparing, operations, decimals
s1-fractii-operatii.subtitle: Extras for fifth grade
theory: Comparing fractions: with the same denominator, the fraction with the greater numerator is greater; with the same numerator, the fraction with the smaller denominator is greater. With different denominators, bring the fractions to the same denominator or cross-multiply: for 3/4 and 5/7 you calculate 3 · 7 = 21 and 5 · 4 = 20, so 3/4 is greater. Trick: compare each fraction with 1/2 or with 1.

Adding and subtracting fractions with different denominators: bring the fractions to a common denominator (the least common multiple of the denominators), then add or subtract the numerators: 1/4 + 1/6 = 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12. Denominators are not added. At the end, simplify the result.

Multiplying fractions: numerator by numerator and denominator by denominator, 2/3 · 4/5 = 8/15; simplify before multiplying. Dividing: multiply the first fraction by the reciprocal of the second fraction (the flipped fraction), 2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 · 5/4 = 10/12 = 5/6. For multiplication and division you do not bring the fractions to the same denominator.

Operations with decimals: for addition and subtraction, line up the decimal points, 2.5 + 0.75 = 3.25. For multiplication, multiply as with natural numbers and give the result as many decimal places as the factors have in total, 1.2 · 0.3 = 0.36. To divide by a decimal, multiply both numbers by 10 or by 100, until the divisor becomes a natural number: 4.5 ÷ 0.5 = 45 ÷ 5 = 9.

s1-completari.title: Prime factors, repeating decimals, proportionality, successive percentages, square roots
s1-completari.subtitle: Arithmetic extras for grades VI and VII
theory: Prime factorization: divide in turn by the smallest prime numbers (2, 3, 5, 7, …) until you get 1; 360 = 2³ · 3² · 5. From the factorization you find the divisors, the GCD (the common factors with their smallest exponents) and the LCM.

Repeating decimals: pure 0.(ab) = ab/99 (as many 9s as the block has digits); mixed 0.c(ab) = (cab − c)/990 (one 9 for each digit of the repeating block, one 0 for each non-repeating digit). A fraction in lowest terms whose denominator has factors 2 or 5 together with other prime factors gives a mixed repeating decimal.

Directly proportional quantities: when one is multiplied by k, the other is multiplied by k too; their ratio is constant (y/x = k). The numbers a, b directly proportional to 3 and 5 are written a = 3k, b = 5k.

Successive increases and decreases (the price goes up by 20%, then goes down by 20%): each percentage applies to the previous price, not to the original one. +20% then −20% does not mean 0%, but −4% (100 → 120 → 96); −10% then −10% means −19%, not −20%. Work with the price 100.
Comparing square roots: bring the numbers under the same radical (5 = √25, 3√2 = √18) and compare the numbers under the radical. Estimating: √50 is between √49 = 7 and √64 = 8, closer to 7.

s1-aprofundare.title: Going deeper: numbers and calculation
s1-aprofundare.subtitle: Special cases in fractions, powers, square roots, ratios, absolute value
theory: The number 1 is neither prime nor composite. 2 is the only even prime number. Watch out for numbers that look prime: 91 = 7 · 13.

Decimal fraction ↔ common fraction: 0.25 = 25/100 = 1/4, and 3/100 = 0.03. A fraction is less than, equal to, or greater than one whole depending on whether the numerator is less than, equal to, or greater than the denominator.
Powers with a negative base: even exponent — positive result, odd exponent — negative result. (−2)² = 4, but (−2)³ = −8.
Square roots: √a · √b = √(a · b) and √a ÷ √b = √(a ÷ b), for a, b ≥ 0 (for division, b ≠ 0), but √a + √b is not √(a + b). Taking factors out from under the square root: √50 = 5√2.
The difference of squares: a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b); this is how you quickly calculate 101 · 99. In a chain of equal ratios, a/3 = b/5 = (a + b)/(3 + 5).

The rule of three: with directly proportional quantities you divide and then multiply; with inversely proportional quantities you multiply and then divide. The equation |x| = a has two solutions if a is positive, one if a = 0 and none if a is negative.

s1-greseala.title: Who calculated correctly?
s1-greseala.subtitle: Four students, four results: find the typical mistakes
theory: As in Part I: four students calculate the same thing and get different results. Each wrong result comes from a typical mistake; look for it so you know how to avoid it.
Powers and signs: −3² = −9 (only 3 is squared), but (−3)² = 9. A negative number to an even power gives a positive result, and to an odd power a negative one; any nonzero number to the power 0 is 1.
Order of operations: first the parentheses, then the powers, then multiplication and division, and finally addition and subtraction.

Fractions: when adding, bring the fractions to a common denominator (the denominators are not added); dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal; 3/4 of a number = the number divided by 4 and multiplied by 3.
Formulas: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², not a² + b²; √(a + b) is not √a + √b: √(9 + 16) = 5, while √9 + √16 = 7; √(x²) = |x|, so the result is never negative.

Percentages and proportions: after a p% price increase and a p% price decrease, the price does NOT return to the original one, because the second time the percentage is taken from the new price; with inversely proportional quantities (workers and days), the product stays the same.
Units: 1 m = 100 cm, but 1 m² = 100 · 100 cm² = 10,000 cm²; the area of a disk is calculated with the radius, not the diameter.
Check: a result can be checked by working backward, by estimating, or by substituting the value you found into the problem.

s2-segmente.title: Segments and midpoints
s2-segmente.subtitle: Segment lengths, the midpoint of a segment
theory: The midpoint M of segment AB splits the segment into two equal parts: AM = MB = AB/2.
If the points are collinear in the order A, B, C, then AC = AB + BC.
Watch out: the midpoint cuts the segment in half; AC = AB + BC only if B lies between A and C.

s2-unghiuri.title: Angles and parallel lines
s2-unghiuri.subtitle: Supplements, complements, corresponding angles, vertical angles
theory: Supplementary angles: they add up to 180°. Complementary angles: they add up to 90°.

When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, corresponding angles are equal, and so are alternate interior angles. Interior angles on the same side of the transversal are supplementary (they add up to 180°).
Vertical angles (formed by two intersecting lines) are equal.
Watch out: complement = 90° − angle; supplement = 180° − angle.

s2-triunghi.title: Triangles: angles, medians, areas
s2-triunghi.subtitle: Angle sum, centroid, area
theory: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°.
The centroid G divides each median in the ratio 2:1 from the vertex (AG = 2/3·AD, GD = 1/3·AD).
Area of a triangle = (base · height) ÷ 2.
Watch out: area = base·height ÷ 2; the angles add up to 180°.
Right triangle: the leg opposite the 30° angle is half the hypotenuse; the median to the hypotenuse is half the hypotenuse.
Equilateral triangle with side ℓ: the height is h = ℓ√3/2, and the area is A = ℓ²√3/4.
In an isosceles triangle, the median to the base is also the altitude and the angle bisector, and the line containing it is the perpendicular bisector of the base.
The measure of an exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the measures of the two interior angles that are not adjacent to it.

s2-paralelogram.title: Parallelograms: perimeter and area
s2-paralelogram.subtitle: Equal opposite sides, perimeter, area
theory: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal.
Perimeter = 2·(a + b), where a and b are the lengths of two adjacent sides.
Area = base · the height to that base.
Watch out: perimeter = 2(L+l); area = base·height.
A rectangle has equal diagonals; a square with side ℓ has the diagonal d = ℓ√2.
A rhombus has perpendicular diagonals; area of a rhombus = d₁ · d₂ ÷ 2.
Trapezoid with bases B and b and height h: midsegment = (B + b) ÷ 2; area of the trapezoid = (B + b) · h ÷ 2.
The sum of the measures of the angles of a convex quadrilateral is 360°.

s2-cerc.title: Circles: angles and radius
s2-cerc.subtitle: Central angle, inscribed angle, diameter
theory: An inscribed angle that intercepts the same arc as a central angle measures half of the central angle.
An inscribed angle subtended by a diameter (a semicircle) measures 90°.
Radius = diameter ÷ 2.
Watch out: circumference L = 2πr, area A = πr² (use the radius, squared for the area).
A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of tangency.
A regular hexagon inscribed in a circle of radius R has sides equal to R, and an inscribed equilateral triangle has sides equal to R√3.

s2-corpuri.title: Solid figures: volume
s2-corpuri.subtitle: Cube, rectangular prism, pyramid, prism
theory: Volume of a cube = l³ (l = edge length). Volume of a rectangular prism = L · l · h (length · width · height). A cube has 6 faces and 12 edges; the total surface area of a cube = 6 · l². A regular tetrahedron has 6 equal edges.
Eighth grade: volume of a pyramid = (base area · height) ÷ 3.

Eighth grade: volume of a right prism = base area · height. Lateral area of a right prism = perimeter of the base · height. Diagonal of a cube = l√3; diagonal of a rectangular prism: d² = L² + l² + h². Angle between two lines that are not in the same plane: replace one of them with a parallel line that intersects the other. The angle you want is the one of at most 90°.
Watch out: volume of a cube = edge³.
Eighth grade: a regular pyramid has lateral surface area = base perimeter · slant height ÷ 2.
Eighth grade: a right circular cone (r = radius of the base, g = slant height, h = height) has lateral surface area = π · r · g and volume = π · r² · h ÷ 3.

s2-unitati.title: Units of measurement: conversions
s2-unitati.subtitle: Lengths, areas, volumes, capacities, masses, and time
theory: Length: km, hm, dam, m, dm, cm, mm — between two neighboring units, the factor is 10 (1 km = 1000 m; 1 m = 100 cm = 1000 mm).
Area: km², hm², dam², m², dm², cm², mm² — between two neighboring units, the factor is 100 (1 m² = 100 dm² = 10,000 cm²); 1 are = 1 dam² = 100 m²; 1 ha = 1 hm² = 10,000 m².
Volume: m³, dm³, cm³, mm³ — between two neighboring units, the factor is 1000 (1 m³ = 1000 dm³; 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³).
Capacity: 1 l = 1 dm³; 1 ml = 1 cm³. Mass: 1 t = 1000 kg; 1 kg = 1000 g. Time: 1 h = 60 min.
Watch out: for areas the factor is 100, and for volumes it is 1000 — not 10!

s2-asemanare.title: Thales's theorem and similarity
s2-asemanare.subtitle: Parallel lines in a triangle, similar triangles, the midsegment
theory: Thales's theorem (the intercept theorem): if MN ∥ BC, with M on AB and N on AC, then AM/MB = AN/NC.
The converse of Thales's theorem: if AM/MB = AN/NC, then MN ∥ BC.
The fundamental theorem of similarity: if MN ∥ BC, then triangle AMN is similar to triangle ABC, so AM/AB = AN/AC = MN/BC.
Similarity criteria for triangles: AA (two pairs of congruent angles), SAS (two pairs of proportional sides, with the angles between them congruent), SSS (all three pairs of sides proportional).
If the similarity ratio is k, the ratio of the perimeters is k, and the ratio of the areas is k².
Midsegment: if M and N are the midpoints of sides AB and AC, then MN ∥ BC and MN = BC ÷ 2.

s2-trigonometrie.title: Right triangle trigonometry
s2-trigonometrie.subtitle: sin, cos, tan, cot, and the values for 30°, 45°, 60°
theory: In triangle ABC with a right angle at A: sin B = opposite leg / hypotenuse = AC/BC; cos B = adjacent leg / hypotenuse = AB/BC.
tan B = opposite leg / adjacent leg = AC/AB; cot B = adjacent leg / opposite leg = AB/AC.
If m(∠B) + m(∠C) = 90°, then sin B = cos C and tan B = cot C.

s2-trapez.title: Trapezoid: midsegment, angles, isosceles, right
s2-trapez.subtitle: One element at a time: bases, segments, angles, lengths and areas
theory: A trapezoid has two parallel sides (the bases B and b) and two non-parallel sides (the legs); the distance between the bases is the height h. Area = (B + b) · h ÷ 2.
The midsegment MN joins the midpoints of the legs, is parallel to the bases, and MN = (B + b) ÷ 2.
The diagonals cut the midsegment at E and F (the midpoints of the diagonals): ME = NF = b ÷ 2, MF = NE = B ÷ 2, and EF = (B − b) ÷ 2.
The two angles on the same leg are supplementary (they add up to 180°).

Isosceles trapezoid: congruent legs, congruent angles at each base, congruent diagonals; the projection of a leg onto the longer base = (B − b) ÷ 2. Conversely, a trapezoid with congruent angles at one base or with congruent diagonals is isosceles.

A right trapezoid has a leg perpendicular to the bases (that leg is the height). If diagonals AC and BD intersect at O (AB ∥ CD), triangles OAB and OCD are similar: OA/OC = OB/OD = AB/CD. If lines AD and BC intersect at O, triangles ODC and OAB are similar, with ratio CD/AB.

s3-trapez-pasi.title: The trapezoid, step by step
s3-trapez-pasi.subtitle: Eight configurations, each with 4–6 steps; the last question is the whole problem
theory: In an isosceles trapezoid, the height comes from the right triangle formed by a leg, the height and the projection (B − b) ÷ 2.
A right trapezoid splits into a rectangle and a right triangle with legs h and B − b.

s2-dreptunghic.title: The right triangle: Pythagoras, 30°, the median, the height
s2-dreptunghic.subtitle: One element at a time: lengths, angles, areas and projections
theory: In triangle ABC, right-angled at A, BC is the hypotenuse (the longest side), and AB and AC are the legs. Pythagorean theorem: BC² = AB² + AC².
The converse: if BC² = AB² + AC², then triangle ABC is right-angled at A.

The leg opposite the 30° angle is half of the hypotenuse; conversely, if a leg is half of the hypotenuse, the angle opposite it measures 30°. In the triangle with angles of 30° and 60°, the other leg is (hypotenuse ÷ 2) · √3.
The isosceles right triangle has acute angles of 45°, and hypotenuse = leg · √2.

The median to the hypotenuse is half of the hypotenuse (the midpoint of the hypotenuse is the center of the circumscribed circle); conversely, if the median AM = BC ÷ 2, the triangle is right-angled at A.
With AD ⊥ BC, D ∈ BC: area = AB · AC ÷ 2 = BC · AD ÷ 2, so AD = AB · AC ÷ BC (the area computed in two ways). Altitude theorem: AD² = BD · DC. Leg theorem: AB² = BD · BC.

s3-dreptunghic-pasi.title: The right triangle step by step
s3-dreptunghic-pasi.subtitle: Eight configurations, each with 4–6 steps; the last question is the whole problem
theory: When you know the legs: first the hypotenuse (Pythagoras), then the area, then the height from the area computed in two ways.
When you have a 30° angle: first the leg opposite it (half of the hypotenuse), then the other leg.

s2-triunghi-general.title: The triangle: types, angles, isosceles, equilateral, congruence, areas
s2-triunghi-general.subtitle: Angles, sides, classifications, congruence and area calculations
theory: The sum of the measures of the angles of a triangle is 180°. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles not next to it.
Triangle inequality: each side is less than the sum of the other two and greater than their difference (|b − c| < a < b + c). The larger angle is opposite the longer side.
By its angles, a triangle is acute, right or obtuse; by its sides, scalene, isosceles or equilateral. If a is the longest side: a² > b² + c² ⇒ obtuse; a² = b² + c² ⇒ right; a² < b² + c² ⇒ acute.
In isosceles triangle ABC with AB = AC, the base angles are congruent (∠B ≡ ∠C), and the height from A is also a median and an angle bisector.
An equilateral triangle has all angles of 60°; with side ℓ: height h = ℓ√3 ÷ 2, area = ℓ²√3 ÷ 4.
Congruence criteria: SAS, ASA, SSS; for right triangles: LL (leg–leg), HL (hypotenuse–leg), LA (leg–acute angle), HA (hypotenuse–acute angle). Two sides and an angle NOT between them are not enough.
Area of a triangle = base · height ÷ 2; area = AB · AC · sin A ÷ 2; Heron's formula (an extension, beyond the curriculum): area = √(p(p − a)(p − b)(p − c)), where p is the semiperimeter.

s3-triunghi-pasi.title: The triangle step by step
s3-triunghi-pasi.subtitle: Seven setups, each with 4–6 steps; the last question is the whole problem
theory: In an isosceles triangle, the height from the apex cuts the base in half: first half of the base, then Pythagoras for the height, then the area.

To find the height to a side, first compute the area another way, then divide: h = 2 · area ÷ side. The type of triangle by its angles, with a the longest side: a² > b² + c² ⇒ obtuse; a² = b² + c² ⇒ right; a² < b² + c² ⇒ acute.

s2-patrulatere.title: Quadrilaterals: parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus, square
s2-patrulatere.subtitle: Sides, angles, diagonals, areas and recognition criteria
theory: The sum of the measures of the angles of a convex quadrilateral is 360°.
A parallelogram has opposite sides parallel and congruent, opposite angles congruent, consecutive angles supplementary (they add up to 180°), and its diagonals bisect each other.

A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if: both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, or both pairs of opposite sides are congruent, or two opposite sides are parallel and congruent, or the diagonals bisect each other, or both pairs of opposite angles are congruent.
Area of a parallelogram = base · its height = AB · AD · sin A, with A acute (if A is obtuse, use its supplement, 180° − A).
A rectangle has congruent diagonals: d = √(L² + l²); their intersection point is the center of the circumscribed circle, with R = d ÷ 2.
A rhombus has all sides congruent, and its diagonals are perpendicular and bisect the angles; area = d₁ · d₂ ÷ 2 = side · height; side² = (d₁ ÷ 2)² + (d₂ ÷ 2)².
A square is both a rectangle and a rhombus: diagonal = ℓ√2, area = ℓ² = d² ÷ 2.

s3-patrulatere-pasi.title: Quadrilaterals step by step
s3-patrulatere-pasi.subtitle: Seven setups with 4–6 steps; the last question is the whole problem
theory: In a rhombus, the diagonals cut each other into perpendicular halves: a quarter of the rhombus is a right triangle with legs d₁ ÷ 2 and d₂ ÷ 2.
The distance from a vertex to a diagonal comes from the area of the triangle computed in two ways.

s2-linii-centre.title: Special lines and centers of a triangle; the midsegment; the angle bisector theorem
s2-linii-centre.subtitle: Medians, angle bisectors, perpendicular bisectors, altitudes, centers and ratios
theory: A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side; the three medians meet at the centroid G, which divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1 from the vertex (AG = 2 · GM).
An angle bisector splits the angle into two congruent angles; the three angle bisectors meet at the center I of the inscribed circle (equally far from the sides).

The perpendicular bisector of a segment is the perpendicular to the segment at its midpoint; every point on it is equally far from the endpoints. The three perpendicular bisectors meet at the center O of the circumscribed circle (OA = OB = OC).
The three altitudes (or their extensions) meet at the orthocenter H. In a right triangle, H is the vertex of the right angle; in an obtuse triangle, H is outside the triangle.
A midsegment joins the midpoints of two sides: MN ∥ BC and MN = BC ÷ 2; the triangle formed by the three midsegments has half the perimeter and one quarter of the area of the original triangle.
Angle bisector theorem: if AD is the bisector of angle A, D ∈ BC, then BD ÷ DC = AB ÷ AC.
In an equilateral triangle, G, I, O and H coincide; R = ℓ√3 ÷ 3 and r = ℓ√3 ÷ 6 (R = 2r).

s3-linii-centre-pasi.title: Lines and centers step by step
s3-linii-centre-pasi.subtitle: Seven setups, with 4–6 steps; the last question is the whole problem
theory: Draw only the points you need. First compute the side or height you need, then use the property of the median, the center or the midsegment.

At the last step, start again from the given data and keep only the calculations you need. For an angle bisector, first find the ratio of the parts, then one part; areas with the same height are in the ratio of the bases.

s2-cerc-poligoane.title: The circle, regular polygons and composite areas
s2-cerc-poligoane.subtitle: Angles, chords, tangents, lengths and areas
theory: A central angle has the measure of the arc between its sides; an inscribed angle measures half of its intercepted arc: an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle.
Congruent chords subtend congruent arcs and are equally far from the center; the diameter perpendicular to a chord passes through its midpoint.
A tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of tangency; the two tangent segments drawn from an exterior point are congruent.

Position of a line relative to a circle of radius r: d > r exterior, d = r tangent, d < r secant (d = the distance from the center to the line). Two circles: compare the distance between the centers with R + r and with R − r.
A cyclic quadrilateral has supplementary opposite angles (their sum is 180°).
Circumference C = 2πr, area of the disk A = πr²; the length of an arc of n° is 2πr · n ÷ 360, and the area of a sector of n° is πr² · n ÷ 360.
Regular polygons inscribed in a circle of radius R: equilateral triangle ℓ = R√3, apothem R ÷ 2; square ℓ = R√2, apothem ℓ ÷ 2; hexagon ℓ = R, apothem ℓ√3 ÷ 2, area = 6 · ℓ²√3 ÷ 4.

s3-cerc-poligoane-pasi.title: The circle step by step
s3-cerc-poligoane-pasi.subtitle: Seven setups; the last step is the whole problem
theory: Identify the radius, the chord or the tangent and look for a right triangle. For regular polygons, join the center to the vertices and use the apothem.
Keep π and square roots in exact form. For a composite area, split the region and add or subtract the areas; at the last step, redo only the calculations you need from the given data.

s2-notiuni.title: Segments, angles and parallel lines
s2-notiuni.subtitle: Basic plane geometry for grades V–VI
theory: The midpoint M of segment AB splits the segment into two congruent segments: AM = MB = AB ÷ 2. If B is between A and C, then AC = AB + BC.
An angle is acute (less than 90°), right (90°), obtuse (between 90° and 180°) or straight (180°). Complementary angles add up to 90°, and supplementary angles add up to 180°.
Vertical angles are congruent. The angles around a point add up to 360°, and adjacent angles formed on a line add up to 180°.
The bisector of an angle splits it into two congruent angles.

Two parallel lines cut by a transversal form congruent alternate interior angles, congruent alternate exterior angles and congruent corresponding angles, and same-side interior angles are supplementary.
Conversely, if two alternate interior (or corresponding) angles are congruent, the lines are parallel. Through a point not on a line there is exactly one parallel to that line.
The perpendicular bisector of a segment is the perpendicular to the segment at its midpoint; every point of the perpendicular bisector is equally far from the endpoints of the segment.

s3-notiuni-pasi.title: Angles and parallels step by step
s3-notiuni-pasi.subtitle: Seven chains; the last step is the whole problem
theory: Identify consecutive segments, adjacent angles, bisectors and the pairs of angles formed by a transversal. For a broken line between parallels, draw the parallel through the inner vertex.
Link each result to the next quantity asked for. For the whole problem, start from the given data and keep only the calculations the final result needs.

s2-completari.title: Parallels, trapezoids, converses, circles: tangents, chords, arcs, composite areas
s2-completari.subtitle: Geometry extras for grades VI and VII
theory: The parallel postulate (Euclid's axiom): through a point not on a line there is exactly one line parallel to that line. Consequences: two lines parallel to a third one are parallel; a line that cuts one of two parallels also cuts the other; a perpendicular to one of two parallels is also perpendicular to the other.
The perimeter of a triangle = the sum of its sides. For an isosceles triangle P = 2 · l + b, for an equilateral one P = 3 · l.

In trapezoid ABCD (AB ∥ CD), the midsegment MN cuts the diagonals at E and F: ME = NF = b ÷ 2, and the segment cut off by the diagonals on the midsegment is EF = (B − b) ÷ 2 (B = the longer base, b = the shorter base); MN = (B + b) ÷ 2.

In a trapezoid, the angles on the same leg are supplementary: m(∠A) + m(∠D) = 180° (same-side interior angles for the transversal AD). In an isosceles trapezoid, the angles at the same base are congruent.
The converse of Thales's theorem (the intercept theorem): if D ∈ AB, E ∈ AC and AD/DB = AE/EC (or AD/AB = AE/AC), then DE ∥ BC. This is how you prove that two lines are parallel using ratios.

In trapezoid ABCD with AB ∥ CD, the diagonals meet at O, and triangles AOB and COD are similar (alternate interior angles): AO/OC = BO/OD = AB/CD — the diagonals of a trapezoid are divided by their intersection point into segments proportional to the bases.

The converse of the Pythagorean theorem: if in a triangle a² + b² = c² (c = the longest side), the triangle is a right triangle, with hypotenuse c. This is how you check whether a triangle is a right triangle: the triples 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25.

An angle inscribed in a semicircle measures 90°: if AB is a diameter and C is on the circle, triangle ABC is right-angled at C. Conversely, the hypotenuse of a right triangle is a diameter of its circumscribed circle, and the center is the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

In the same circle: congruent chords ↔ congruent arcs, and congruent chords are equally distant from the center. A central angle has the measure of the arc between its sides; a chord equal to the radius subtends an arc of 60°.
A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency. Tangents from an external point are congruent (PA = PB), and OP is the bisector of angle APB.

The positions of a line relative to a circle, by the distance d from the center to the line: d > r — outside the circle (no common point), d = r — tangent (1 point), d < r — a secant of the circle (2 points).

Two circles with radii R > r and distance d between their centers: outside each other (d > R + r), externally tangent (d = R + r), intersecting (R − r < d < R + r), internally tangent (d = R − r), one inside the other (d < R − r).
Circumference L = 2πr; the length of an arc of n° is L · n ÷ 360 = π · r · n ÷ 180. The area of a sector of n° is πr² · n ÷ 360.

The area of a composite figure: split the composite figure into known figures (rectangles, triangles, disks, sectors) and add the areas, or subtract the area of the cut-out part from the area of the large figure (the shaded region). The results stay exact, with π and radicals: 16 − 4π, 36 + 9√3.

s2-aprofundare.title: Going deeper: geometry
s2-aprofundare.subtitle: Special cases in triangles, trapezoids, circles, areas
theory: Triangle inequality: three lengths can be the sides of a triangle only if the greatest is strictly less than the sum of the other two. In case of equality (2, 5, 7), the points are collinear.
Right triangles have four congruence cases: LL (leg–leg), HL (hypotenuse–leg), LA (leg–acute angle) and HA (hypotenuse–acute angle). Equal angles alone are not enough.

In a trapezoid, the part of the midsegment between the diagonals is half the difference of the bases. In an isosceles trapezoid, the projection of a non-parallel side onto the longer base is also half the difference of the bases.
The converse of Thales's theorem (the intercept theorem): if AD/DB = AE/EC, then DE ∥ BC. The altitude theorem in the right triangle: AD² = BD · DC.
In the same circle, congruent chords have congruent arcs and vice versa. A quadrilateral is cyclic if the opposite angles add up to 180°; the rectangle and the isosceles trapezoid are cyclic.
Heron's formula (an extension, beyond the curriculum): area = √(p(p − a)(p − b)(p − c)), where p is the semiperimeter of the triangle.

s2-cub.title: The cube and the rectangular prism
s2-cub.subtitle: Elements, areas, volumes, diagonals, nets, angles and distances
theory: A cube has 8 vertices, 12 equal edges and 6 congruent square faces. A rectangular prism also has 8 vertices, 12 edges and 6 faces, but its faces are rectangles; a cube is a rectangular prism with all its edges equal. The usual notation is ABCDA′B′C′D′: the base ABCD is at the bottom, and A′ is above A (sometimes it is written ABCDEFGH).

The cube with edge l: the sum of the edges is 12 · l, the lateral surface area 4 · l² (four faces), the total surface area 6 · l² (six faces), the volume l³. For an edge of 5 cm: the sum of the edges is 60 cm, the lateral surface area 100 cm², the total surface area 150 cm², the volume 125 cm³. Watch out: don't confuse the lateral surface area with the total surface area, or the area with the volume.

The rectangular prism with dimensions a, b, c (length, width, height): the sum of the edges is 4 · (a + b + c), the lateral surface area 2 · (a + b) · c (the perimeter of the base multiplied by the height), the total surface area 2 · (ab + bc + ac), the volume a · b · c.

The diagonal of a face of the cube is l√2, and the diagonal of the cube is l√3. For the rectangular prism, the diagonal of the base is √(a² + b²), and the diagonal of the prism is √(a² + b² + c²); for 3 cm, 4 cm and 12 cm: √(9 + 16 + 144) = √169 = 13 cm. The 4 diagonals are equal and bisect each other at the center of the solid.

The net of the cube is made of 6 squares; the cube has 11 different nets. In a straight row of squares, two faces separated by exactly one square end up opposite each other. Five squares in a row, or four squares arranged as a bigger square, cannot be folded into a cube.

The diagonal section ACC′A′ of the cube is a rectangle with sides l√2 and l. Triangle A′BD has face diagonals as all its sides, so it is equilateral. Any section parallel to the base is congruent to the base.

Units of volume: 1 dm³ means 1 liter, and 1 cm³ means 1 ml. Between neighboring cubic units, the factor is 1000: 1 m³ contains 1000 dm³, and 1 dm³ contains 1000 cm³. Convert all the dimensions to the same unit before multiplying.

A cube cut into n · n · n equal small cubes and painted on the outside: 8 small cubes have three painted faces (the corner ones); 12 · (n − 2) have two; 6 · (n − 2)² have one; (n − 2)³ have none. For 27 small cubes: 8 + 12 + 6 + 1 = 27.

Two lines in space can be parallel, intersecting or skew (they have no common points and are not parallel, like AB and CC′ in the cube). To find the angle between two skew lines, move one of them to a parallel line that intersects the other line. The angle between two lines is between 0° and 90°, never 120°.

The angle between a line and a plane is the angle between the line and its projection onto the plane: for the diagonal AC′ of the cube and the base, the projection is AC, and the angle is ∠C′AC. A line perpendicular to the plane makes 90° with it; a parallel one makes 0°. A line is perpendicular to a plane if it is perpendicular to two intersecting lines in the plane.

The angle between two planes: choose a point on their common line and draw a perpendicular to it in each plane; the angle between these perpendiculars is the angle between the planes. In the cube, the planes (ABC′) and (ABC) form an angle of 45°: it is ∠C′BC.

The distance from a point to a plane is measured along the perpendicular from the point to the plane. The volume trick: you calculate the volume of the same pyramid in two ways, and the distance is three times the volume divided by the area of the base. In the cube, the distance from A to the plane (A′BD) is one third of the diagonal AC′.

Theorem of three perpendiculars: if A′A is perpendicular to the plane of the base and AM is perpendicular to the line BD in the base, then A′M is perpendicular to BD. This is how you find the distance from a top vertex to a line in the base, using the Pythagorean theorem in triangle A′AM.

Practical problems: when painting a room, you add the walls (the lateral surface area) and the ceiling, then subtract the doors and windows; a box without a lid means the total surface area minus one base; paint, cans and tiles are bought whole, so you round up.

s2-piramida.title: The regular pyramid and the regular tetrahedron
s2-piramida.subtitle: Apothems, edges, areas, volumes, angles and distances
theory: A pyramid has a base (a polygon) and an apex V outside the plane of the base; the lateral faces are triangles. A pyramid whose base is a polygon with n sides has n + 1 vertices, 2n edges and n + 1 faces: a quadrilateral pyramid has 5 vertices, 8 edges and 5 faces, and a triangular pyramid (the tetrahedron) has 4 vertices, 6 edges and 4 faces.

A regular pyramid has a base that is a regular polygon, and the foot of the height is the center O of the base: for a square, the intersection of the diagonals; for an equilateral triangle, the centroid. The lateral edges are equal, and the lateral faces are congruent isosceles triangles.

The slant height of the pyramid (VM, with M the midpoint of a side of the base) is the height of a lateral face. The apothem of the base (OM) is the distance from the center to a side: for a square with side l, OM = l ÷ 2 and OA = l√2 ÷ 2; for an equilateral triangle, OM is one third of the height, and OA two thirds.

Three right triangles solve almost any regular pyramid: VOM (VM² = VO² + OM²), VOA (VA² = VO² + OA²) and VMB, in the lateral face (VB² = VM² + MB²). Watch out: with OM you find the slant height, with OA you find the lateral edge.

Lateral surface area = perimeter of the base · slant height ÷ 2 (the sum of the areas of the lateral faces); total surface area = lateral surface area + area of the base. For a base side of 6 cm and a slant height of 5 cm: the lateral surface area is 60 cm², the area of the base 36 cm², the total surface area 96 cm².

Volume of the pyramid = area of the base · height ÷ 3, that is, one third of the volume of the prism with the same base and the same height. The most common trap: forgetting to divide by 3. For a base side of 6 cm and a height of 4 cm, the volume is 48 cm³.

A regular square pyramid with all edges equal to l: the lateral faces are equilateral, triangle VAC is an isosceles right triangle with the right angle at V, the height is equal to OA (l√2 ÷ 2), and the lateral edge makes an angle of 45° with the base.

A regular tetrahedron has all 6 edges equal to l and 4 equilateral faces: total surface area l²√3, height l√6 ÷ 3, volume l³√2 ÷ 12. Opposite edges are perpendicular. A regular triangular pyramid whose lateral edge is different from the base side is not a regular tetrahedron.

The angle between a lateral edge and the base is ∠VAO (the projection of VA onto the base is AO), and its tangent is VO ÷ OA. The dihedral angle between a lateral face and the base is ∠VMO, with tangent VO ÷ OM.

The opposite faces (VAD) and (VBC) of the quadrilateral pyramid intersect along a line through V, parallel to AD; their angle is ∠RVM, where R and M are the midpoints of AD and BC. If the slant height is equal to the base side, triangle RVM is equilateral, and the angle is 60°.

The distance from the center O of the base to a lateral face VBC is OT, the altitude to the hypotenuse in triangle VOM: OT = VO · OM ÷ VM (BC is perpendicular to the plane VOM). The distance from the vertex A of the base to the face VBC is twice that, because O is the midpoint of AC.

A section parallel to the base, through the midpoint of the height, is a polygon similar to the base, with sides half as long: its area is one quarter of the area of the base, and the small pyramid on top has one eighth of the volume.

s2-prisma.title: The right prism and the regular prism
s2-prisma.subtitle: Bases, areas, volumes, diagonals, angles and distances
theory: A prism has two bases, congruent polygons in parallel planes, and its lateral faces are parallelograms. A prism whose base is a polygon with n sides has 2n vertices, 3n edges and n + 2 faces: a triangular prism has 6 vertices, 9 edges and 5 faces.

A right prism has its lateral edges perpendicular to the bases: the lateral faces are rectangles, and the height is equal to the lateral edge. A regular prism is a right prism whose base is a regular polygon: the regular triangular prism has an equilateral triangle as its base, and the regular square prism has a square as its base. The problem may describe the solid without naming it: “the right prism whose base is an equilateral triangle”.

Areas of the regular bases: the equilateral triangle with side l has area l²√3 ÷ 4 and height l√3 ÷ 2; the square has area l²; the regular hexagon can be divided into 6 equilateral triangles, so its area is 6 · l²√3 ÷ 4, and its long diagonal is 2l.

Lateral surface area of a right prism = perimeter of the base · height; total surface area = lateral surface area + 2 · area of the base (there are two bases). Volume of the prism = area of the base · height, with no division by 3 (that is for the pyramid).

The diagonal of a lateral face is found with the Pythagorean theorem in the rectangle of the face: for a base side of 6 cm and a height of 8 cm, the diagonal is 10 cm. The diagonal of the regular square prism: AC′² = AC² + CC′², with AC = l√2.
The angle between a lateral face diagonal and the base: the projection of B′ onto the base is B, so the angle between the line AB′ and the base is ∠B′AB, with tangent BB′ ÷ AB.

The angle between a line and a LATERAL FACE of the regular triangular prism: the projection of the vertex A onto the plane (BCC′) is the midpoint M of BC, because AM ⊥ BC and AM ⊥ BB′. So the angle between the line AB′ and the face (BCC′) is ∠AB′M.
The angle between the planes (ABC′) and (ABC): on the common edge AB, from the midpoint K, CK ⊥ AB in the base and C′K ⊥ AB in the plane (ABC′); the angle is ∠C′KC, with tangent CC′ ÷ CK.

The distance from the vertex A to the opposite lateral face (BCC′) is AM, the altitude of the equilateral triangle of the base. The distance from C to the plane (ABC′) is the altitude to the hypotenuse in triangle C′CK: CK · CC′ ÷ C′K.
The section of a prism by a plane parallel to the bases is congruent to the base. The diagonal section ACC′A′ of the regular square prism is a rectangle with sides AC and AA′.

s2-spatiu.title: Points, lines and planes in space
s2-spatiu.subtitle: Positions, parallelism, perpendicularity, projections, angles, distances
theory: The primary notions of solid geometry are the point, the line and the plane. Through two distinct points there passes only one line. A plane is determined by: three non-collinear points, a line and a point not on it, two intersecting lines, or two distinct parallel lines. If two points of a line lie in a plane, the line is contained in the plane.

Two lines can be coincident, intersecting (one common point), parallel (coplanar, with no common points) or skew (with no common points and not parallel). A line can be contained in a plane, parallel to it, or intersecting it (one common point). Two planes can be coincident, parallel or intersecting (they have a common line).

The parallel postulate: through a point not on a line there passes only one parallel to it. Two lines parallel to a third line are parallel to each other. The line–plane criterion: a line not contained in a plane, parallel to a line in the plane, is parallel to the plane; a plane that contains a line parallel to another plane cuts it along a parallel to that line.

The criterion for parallel planes: a plane that contains two intersecting lines (lines that cut each other) parallel to another plane is parallel to it. Any line in one of two parallel planes is parallel to the other; two parallel planes cut by a third plane give parallel lines; through a point not in a plane there passes only one plane parallel to it.

A line perpendicular to a plane is perpendicular to any line in the plane; the criterion: it is enough for it to be perpendicular to two intersecting lines in the plane. Through a point there passes only one perpendicular to a plane and only one plane perpendicular to a line. Two lines perpendicular to the same plane are parallel; a parallel to a perpendicular to a plane is also perpendicular to it.

Two planes perpendicular to the same line are parallel; a line perpendicular to one of two parallel planes is also perpendicular to the other. The projection of a point onto a plane is the foot of the perpendicular from the point; the perpendicular is the shortest segment from the point to the plane, and its length is the distance from the point to the plane.

The distance between a line parallel to a plane and the plane, the distance between two parallel planes, and the distance between two parallel lines are measured along a common perpendicular (from any point). A segment parallel to a plane projects onto a parallel segment of the same length; a line perpendicular to the plane projects onto a point.
Theorem of three perpendiculars: PA ⊥ α, AM ⊥ d (d in α) ⇒ PM ⊥ d. The first converse: PA ⊥ α, PM ⊥ d ⇒ AM ⊥ d. The second converse: PM ⊥ d, AM ⊥ d and PA ⊥ AM ⇒ PA ⊥ α.

The angle between a line and a plane is the angle with its projection onto the plane: 0° if the line is parallel to the plane or contained in it, 90° if it is perpendicular. The angle with the plane and the angle with the normal to the plane are complementary. The length of the projection of a segment = the length of the segment · the cosine of the angle with the plane.

A dihedral angle is formed by two half-planes with the same edge; it is measured by the plane angle: from the same point of the edge, a perpendicular to the edge is drawn in each face. A dihedral angle can be acute, right or obtuse; two adjacent dihedral angles whose outer faces form a plane have supplementary plane angles.

The criterion for perpendicular planes: a plane that contains a line perpendicular to another plane is perpendicular to it. The converse: in two perpendicular planes, a line in one of them that is perpendicular to their common line is perpendicular to the other plane. The common line of two intersecting planes that are perpendicular to a third plane is perpendicular to that plane.

s2-rotunde.title: The cylinder, the cone and the sphere
s2-rotunde.subtitle: Sections, nets, areas, volumes, composite solids
theory: Round solids are obtained by rotating a plane figure around an axis: a rectangle around one side gives the cylinder, a right triangle around one leg gives the cone, a half-disk around its diameter gives the ball. They are not polyhedra.

The right circular cylinder has two bases, congruent disks in parallel planes, with radius R; the generatrix is equal to the height h. The axial section is a rectangle with sides 2R and h (a square when h = 2R); the section parallel to the bases is a disk with radius R.
The net of the cylinder: a rectangle with sides 2πR and h, plus two disks with radius R. Lateral surface area A_l = 2πRh; total surface area A_t = 2πRh + 2πR² = 2πR(R + h); volume V = πR²h.
The right circular cone has vertex V, a base that is a disk with center O and radius R, height VO = h and slant height G = VA (A on the circle of the base). In the right triangle VOA: G² = h² + R².

The axial section of the cone is the isosceles triangle VAB, with base AB = 2R, equal sides G and height h; its area is R · h. Equilateral ⇔ G = 2R (then h = R√3, the angle between the slant height and the base is 60°); right-angled at V ⇔ h = R (then G = R√2, the angle is 45°).
