The net of the lateral surface of the cone is a circular sector with radius G; its arc is as long as the circumference of the base, 2πR, so the angle of the sector is 360° · R ÷ G.
The cone: lateral surface area A_l = πRG, total surface area A_t = πRG + πR² = πR(R + G), volume V = πR²h ÷ 3 — one third of the volume of the cylinder with the same base and the same height.

The sphere with center O and radius R: the points at distance R from O; the ball: the points at a distance of at most R. A plane at distance d from the center: d greater than R — no common point; d = R — tangent plane (perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact); d less than R — the section is a circle with radius r, where r² = R² − d²; d = 0 — great circle.
Area of the sphere A = 4πR² (4 times the area of the great disk); volume of the ball V = 4πR³ ÷ 3. The solid hemisphere: volume 2πR³ ÷ 3, total surface area 2πR² + πR² = 3πR².

Watch out: don't put the diameter in place of the radius; the lateral surface area doesn't include the bases; for the cone and the ball, don't forget to divide by 3; for the cone, the lateral surface area uses the slant height, not the height; a container without a lid has a single base.

Composite solids: the volumes (and the areas of the visible parts) are added or subtracted. When a liquid is poured from one container into another, or a solid is melted and reshaped, the volume stays the same. 1 dm³ = 1 l, 1 cm³ = 1 ml.
If the radius of a ball doubles, the area becomes 4 times larger and the volume 8 times larger; the ball inscribed in a cylinder takes up two thirds of its volume (Archimedes).

s2-trunchi.title: Frustums and sections parallel to the base
s2-trunchi.subtitle: Similarity, the frustum of a pyramid, the frustum of a cone
theory: A plane parallel to the base of a pyramid (or of a cone) cuts off a small solid, similar to the large one. The similarity ratio k is read on the heights (from the vertex!), on the lateral edges or on the slant heights: k is the ratio between the distance from the vertex to the section and the height.

For similar solids with ratio k: lengths are multiplied by k, areas (including the area of the section compared to the area of the base) by k², volumes by k³. Example: plane through the midpoint of the height ⇒ k = 1/2, area of the section = 1/4 of the base, small solid = 1/8 of the volume.

The frustum of a pyramid is the part between the base and a section parallel to the base. The bases are similar polygons in parallel planes; in a regular frustum, the lateral faces are congruent isosceles trapezoids. Height = distance between the bases; slant height = height of a lateral face.

For the frustum of a regular square pyramid with sides L and l and height h: slant height² = h² + ((L − l) ÷ 2)²; lateral edge² = h² + (difference between the half-diagonals)², that is, h² + ((L − l)√2 ÷ 2)².

The frustum of a pyramid: lateral surface area = sum of the areas of the trapezoids = (perimeter of the larger base + perimeter of the smaller base) · slant height ÷ 2; total surface area = lateral surface area + B + b; volume V = h · (B + b + √(B · b)) ÷ 3, where B and b are the areas of the bases.

The frustum of a cone has as its bases two disks with radii R and r, in parallel planes; it is obtained by rotating a right trapezoid around the side perpendicular to the bases. The axial section is an isosceles trapezoid with bases 2R and 2r; the slant height: G² = h² + (R − r)².
The frustum of a cone: lateral surface area A_l = πG(R + r); total surface area A_t = πG(R + r) + πR² + πr²; volume V = πh(R² + r² + R · r) ÷ 3.

The difference method: volume of the frustum = volume of the large solid − volume of the small solid that was cut off. When the slant heights (or the lateral edges) are extended, they meet at the vertex of the original solid; the height x of the small solid is found from the similarity: x ÷ (x + h) = r ÷ R.
The pyramid (cone) has one third of the volume of the prism (cylinder) with the same base and the same height.

Watch out: the ratio is taken from the vertex, not from the base; the area of the section is multiplied by k², not by k; in the volume of the frustum, don't leave out the term √(B · b) (or R · r, respectively) or the division by 3; for the slant height of the frustum, the horizontal leg is (L − l) ÷ 2; a bucket or a flowerpot without a lid has a single base (the bottom = the smaller base).

s3-text.title: Word problems (systems)
s3-text.subtitle: Solved with equations / systems
theory: Fifth and sixth grades: bar model method, comparison method, unit method, working backwards, or an equation with one unknown. Seventh and eighth grades: use letters (x, y) for the unknowns, write the equations from the problem, and solve the system by substitution or elimination.
At the end, check the solution against the problem.
Watch out: the answer must make sense (a whole number of objects or people); if you get a fraction or a negative number, check the equation and your calculations again.

s3-expresii.title: Algebraic expressions
s3-expresii.subtitle: Special product formulas
theory: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²;  (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b².
a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b) — difference of squares.
Spot the right formula and use it to calculate quickly.

s3-functii.title: Functions
s3-functii.subtitle: The linear function, its graph, intersections with the axes
theory: The graph of the function f: ℝ → ℝ, f(x) = ax + b is a straight line (on an interval, the graph is a line segment, and on a finite set, it consists of points).
Intersection with the x-axis (Ox): solve f(x) = 0. Intersection with the y-axis (Oy): calculate f(0) = b.
To calculate f(x), replace x with the given value.

s3-cerc.title: Circles: chord, radius, Pythagoras
s3-cerc.subtitle: Radius perpendicular to a chord, circumference, area
theory: A radius perpendicular to a chord passes through the midpoint of the chord.
If O is the center of the circle, AB is a chord, and M is its midpoint, then OM is the distance from the center to the chord and r² = OM² + (AB ÷ 2)² (the Pythagorean theorem).
Circumference of a circle: L = 2πr. Area of a disk: A = πr².
Regular polygons inscribed in a circle of radius R: the equilateral triangle has side ℓ = R√3, and the square has side ℓ = R√2.

Apothem: for the square, a = ℓ ÷ 2; for the equilateral triangle, a = ℓ√3/6. In right triangle ABC (m(∠A) = 90°), with AD ⊥ BC: AD = AB · AC ÷ BC (the area in two ways) and AB² = BD · BC (leg theorem). The centroid G divides the median AM so that AG = 2 · GM, that is, GM = AM ÷ 3.

s3-paralelogram.title: Parallelograms and midsegments
s3-paralelogram.subtitle: Perimeter, area, midsegment
theory: Perimeter of a parallelogram = 2·(a + b). Area = base · height. The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. Area of a trapezoid = (B + b) · h ÷ 2, where B and b are the bases and h is the height. Area of a rhombus = d₁ · d₂ ÷ 2 (its diagonals are perpendicular).
The midsegment of a triangle joins the midpoints of two sides and is equal to half of the third side.
Metric relations in triangle ABC with a right angle at A, AD ⊥ BC, and D ∈ BC: AD² = BD · DC (the altitude theorem) and AB² = BD · BC (the leg theorem).
The altitude to the hypotenuse: AD = AB · AC ÷ BC.

s3-corpuri.title: Solid figures: surface area and volume
s3-corpuri.subtitle: Prism, cube, pyramid
theory: Right prism: lateral surface area = base perimeter · height; volume = base area · height.
Cube with edge l: total surface area = 6·l², volume = l³. Diagonal of a rectangular prism: d² = L² + l² + h² (for a cube, d = l√3).

Pyramid: volume = (base area · height) ÷ 3. Regular pyramid: lateral area = (base perimeter · slant height) ÷ 2; the slant height VM is found with the Pythagorean theorem in triangle VOM (O is the center of the base, M the midpoint of a side of the base).

The distance from a point to a plane is measured along the perpendicular drawn from the point to the plane. You can also find it from the volume: for a pyramid, the distance from the apex to the plane of the base = 3 · volume ÷ base area. Angle between two lines that are not in the same plane: replace one of them with a parallel line that intersects the other. The angle you want is the one of at most 90°.
Theorem of three perpendiculars: if AB ⊥ plane, B is in the plane, and BC ⊥ d (d in the plane, C on d), then AC ⊥ d.
A regular tetrahedron has all its edges equal, and its faces are equilateral triangles.

s3-calcul-algebric.title: Algebraic calculation: powers, like terms, special products, factoring, rational expressions
s3-calcul-algebric.subtitle: Exercises for grades V–VIII
theory: Powers: aᵐ · aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐ·ⁿ, (a · b)ⁿ = aⁿ · bⁿ. Careful: −3² = −9, but (−3)² = 9; (−1)ⁿ is 1 for even n and −1 for odd n.

Like terms have the same variable part (the same letters with the same exponents): 3x and −5x are like terms, 3x and 3x² are not. To combine them, add the coefficients; the variable part stays the same.
Special product formulas: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b², (a − b)(a + b) = a² − b². Careful: (a + b)² is not a² + b².
Common factor: ab + ac = a(b + c). Take out the greatest common divisor of the coefficients and each common letter with its smallest exponent.
Factoring: first the common factor, then the formulas (a² − b², a² ± 2ab + b²), then grouping the terms; x² + (p + q)x + p · q = (x + p)(x + q).
A rational expression is defined only if its denominator is not 0: the values that make the denominator zero are excluded. Only common factors cancel (after factoring), never terms.
To multiply rational expressions, multiply the numerators and the denominators; to divide, multiply by the reciprocal of the second one; to add or subtract, use a common denominator.

s3-expresii-pasi.title: The expression E(x) step by step
s3-expresii-pasi.subtitle: Eight chains; the last step is the whole problem
theory: For E(x): factor the numerator and the denominator, write down the excluded values, cancel the common factors, and only then compute values.

For E(n) to be an integer, write E(n) = an integer + k/(n − a); then n − a is an integer divisor of k. At the end, remove the excluded values. Minimum value: write E(x) = (x − p)² + q; since (x − p)² ≥ 0, E(x) ≥ q, with equality at x = p. Sums: 1/(n(n + 1)) = 1/n − 1/(n + 1), and in a sum the middle terms cancel out. In an equation with E(x), after multiplying by the denominator, check each solution against the domain.

s3-probleme-functii.title: Problems with equations, functions and coordinates
s3-probleme-functii.subtitle: Exercises for grades VI–VIII
theory: In a word problem, you name the unknown, write the equation from the statement, solve it and check the answer in all the conditions of the problem.

For “Is it possible?”, assume that the given value is correct and calculate: if you get a number that does not fit (not whole, negative or different from the one in the statement), the answer is “no”.
The graph of the function f(x) = ax + b meets the Ox axis at the point where f(x) = 0 and the Oy axis at the point (0, b). The point (m, n) is on the graph if f(m) = n.

The distance between A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂) is found with the Pythagorean theorem: AB² = (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)². The midpoint of AB has the coordinates ((x₁ + x₂) ÷ 2, (y₁ + y₂) ÷ 2). The point symmetric to A(x, y) with respect to the Ox axis is (x, −y), with respect to the Oy axis it is (−x, y), and with respect to the origin O it is (−x, −y).

s3-probleme-functii-pasi.title: Problems and functions step by step
s3-probleme-functii-pasi.subtitle: Eight chains; the last step is the whole problem
theory: For a function: first find the points on the axes (f(x) = 0 and f(0)), then the lengths, the area of the triangle with the axes and, writing the area in two ways, the distance from O to the line.
For a word problem: name the unknown, write the equation, solve it and check the result in every sentence of the statement.

s3-gradul2-functii.title: The incomplete quadratic equation and the function through two points
s3-gradul2-functii.subtitle: Extras for eighth grade
theory: The incomplete quadratic equation: x² = 9 has two solutions, x = 3 and x = −3 (do not forget the negative solution); x² = 0 has a single solution; x² = −4 has no real solutions. Without a constant term: x² − 5x = 0 can be written as x(x − 5) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 5; do not divide by x, because you lose the solution 0. By factoring: x² − 9 = 0 can be written as (x − 3)(x + 3) = 0.

To find the function f(x) = ax + b from two points of its graph, substitute the coordinates of the points: A(1, 5) and B(3, 9) give a + b = 5 and 3a + b = 9. Subtract the two relations: 2a = 4, so a = 2 and b = 3, that is f(x) = 2x + 3. Shortcut: a is the difference of the values divided by the difference of the x-coordinates, (9 − 5) ÷ (3 − 1) = 2. At the end, check both points.

s3-functii-domeniu.title: The domain and codomain of a function
s3-functii-domeniu.subtitle: When f(x) exists, when a point is on the graph, the shape of the graph
theory: The notation f: A → B shows the domain A (the numbers for which the function is defined) and the codomain B (the set that contains the values). f(a) exists only if a is in A. A point M(a, b) is on the graph only if a is in the domain and f(a) = b; if a is not in the domain, the point is not on the graph, even if the formula fits.

All the values of the function must be in the codomain. The equation f(x) = y has a solution only if the solution x is in the domain. For f(x) = ax + b, the shape of the graph depends on the domain: a finite set gives separate points, a closed interval gives a segment, an interval unbounded on one side gives a ray, and ℝ gives a line.
An expression with a division makes no sense where the divisor is 0: 6 ÷ (x − 2) makes no sense for x = 2. Such values are removed from the domain.

s3-cub-pasi.title: The cube and the rectangular prism step by step
s3-cub-pasi.subtitle: Eleven chains; the last step is the whole problem
theory: How to solve a problem with solids in steps: draw the solid with its base at the bottom and mark the given data; look for the hidden right triangles (a vertical edge is perpendicular to every line in the base); find the lengths one by one, with the Pythagorean theorem; only at the end answer the hard question (distance, angle, volume).

The distance from a point to a plane, three methods: construct the perpendicular (perpendicular to two intersecting lines in the plane); use the theorem of three perpendiculars and the altitude of a right triangle (the product of the legs divided by the hypotenuse); calculate the volume in two ways. If the plane passes through the midpoint of a segment, the endpoints of the segment are at the same distance from the plane.

The angle between a line and the base: project the top endpoint onto the base and work in the resulting right triangle, with the tangent, the sine or the cosine. Conversely, from the angle you find the height: at 45° the height is equal to the projection, and at 60° it is the projection multiplied by √3.

s3-piramida-pasi.title: The pyramid step by step
s3-piramida-pasi.subtitle: Chains of steps; the last step is the whole problem
theory: How to solve a regular pyramid problem in steps: draw the pyramid with the base at the bottom and the height VO; first find the elements of the base (OM, OA, the area of the base); then, from the right triangles VOM, VOA, VMB, the slant height, the height or the lateral edge; only at the end the areas, the volume, the angles or the distances.

The distance from a point to a lateral face: either construct the perpendicular (OT to VM, with BC perpendicular to the plane VOM), or use the volume of the same pyramid calculated in two ways: the distance is three times the volume, divided by the area of the face.

The angle between two lines with no common point is found by moving one of them to a parallel line, usually a midsegment: in a regular tetrahedron, the midsegments parallel to two opposite edges are perpendicular.

s3-prisma-pasi.title: The prism step by step
s3-prisma-pasi.subtitle: Chains of steps; the last step is the whole problem
theory: How to solve a regular prism problem in steps: first find the elements of the base (the area, the altitude of the equilateral triangle, the diagonal of the square), then what belongs to the lateral faces (rectangles), then the diagonals, and at the end the volume, the angles or the distances.

The distance from a point to a slanted plane of the prism: find a plane perpendicular to a line in the given plane (for example the plane CMN, perpendicular to A′B′) and work in it: the distance is the altitude to the hypotenuse of a right triangle.

The angle between a line and a lateral face: project a vertex of the base onto the lateral face (in the regular triangular prism, A projects onto the midpoint of BC) and work in the resulting right triangle.

s3-spatiu-pasi.title: Proofs in space step by step
s3-spatiu-pasi.subtitle: Chains of steps; the last step is the whole problem
theory: A proof in space is done in steps: you name the plane figure that gives the parallelism or the perpendicularity (a rectangle, an isosceles triangle), then you apply the right criterion, which requires two intersecting lines, that is, lines that cut each other, both for parallel planes and for a line perpendicular to a plane.

For the angle between two planes: you first find their common line (the edge of the dihedral angle), then a perpendicular to it, from the same point, in each plane; the angle between them is the angle between the planes.

For the distance between two parallel planes, choose a line perpendicular to both (in the cube, the diagonal) and measure along it; for the distance between two parallel lines, look for a common perpendicular.

s3-rotunde-pasi.title: Round solids step by step
s3-rotunde-pasi.subtitle: Chains of steps; the last step is the whole problem
theory: The problem in steps: first find the missing elements (the radius, the height, the slant height) from the right plane figure — the axial section, the right triangle VOA or the net — then apply the formula for the area or the volume.
The last step goes back to the whole problem: write the result as a multiple of π (for example 96π cm³), without replacing π with an approximate value, unless asked otherwise.

s3-trunchi-pasi.title: Frustums step by step
s3-trunchi-pasi.subtitle: Chains of steps; the last step is the whole problem
theory: The problem in steps: first find the missing element from the right plane figure (the right triangle with legs h and (L − l) ÷ 2 and the slant height as hypotenuse; the right triangle with legs h and R − r and hypotenuse G; the similarity between the small solid and the large one), then apply the formulas.
The last step goes back to the whole problem; also check the result with the difference method (large solid − small solid) when possible.

s3-ecuatia.title: Build the equation
s3-ecuatia.subtitle: Choose the right equation, solve it, answer the question
theory: Build the equation (Part III): choose the unknown x, write the other quantities using x, then turn the condition in the problem into an equality.
Watch the words: “5 more” means x + 5, “5 times as many” means 5 · x; half of x is x/2, a quarter is x/4; “the rest” is what is left after subtraction.
Ages grow the same way for everyone: in n years, each person is n years older; double the son's age is written with parentheses: 2(x + n).
The perimeter of a rectangle adds all four sides: 2 · (length + width). With hens and rabbits, count the legs: 2 for a hen, 4 for a rabbit.
The percentage is taken from the quantity the problem talks about: a 20% discount on the original price x is 20/100 · x.
After you solve the equation, answer exactly the question of the problem (it may ask for a number other than x) and check the result in the problem.

solution: 52,481 is between 52,000 and 53,000; the hundreds digit is 4 ⇒ down: 52,000.

nr-60.statement: Which number becomes 80 when rounded to the nearest ten?
hints: Round each number and compare it with 80.
solution: 76 is between 70 and 80, with ones digit 6 ⇒ 80. (74 becomes 70, and 85 and 86 become 90.)

nr-61.statement: What is the smallest natural number that becomes 700 when rounded to the nearest hundred?
hints: Which numbers before 700 round up to 700?
solution: The numbers from 650 to 749 become 700 when rounded to the nearest hundred (649 becomes 600) ⇒ the smallest is 650.

nr-62.statement: What number is written in Roman numerals: XIV?
hints: A smaller numeral placed before a larger one is subtracted; placed after it, it is added.
solution: X means 10, and IV means 4 (I before V: 5 − 1) ⇒ 10 + 4 = 14.

nr-63.statement: What number is written in Roman numerals: XXIX?
hints: A smaller numeral placed before a larger one is subtracted; placed after it, it is added.

nr-64.statement: What number is written in Roman numerals: XLVII?
hints: A smaller numeral placed before a larger one is subtracted; placed after it, it is added.

nr-65.statement: What number is written in Roman numerals: CDXC?
hints: A smaller numeral placed before a larger one is subtracted; placed after it, it is added.

nr-66.statement: How is the number 9 written in Roman numerals?
hints: 9 is 1 less than 10.

nr-67.statement: How is the year 2026 written in Roman numerals?
hints: Write the thousands, the tens and the ones in turn.
solution: MM means 2000, XX means 20, VI means 6 ⇒ MMXXVI.

fr-01.statement: What part of the circle is colored?
hints: Into how many equal parts is the circle divided?
solution: The circle has 2 equal parts and one is colored ⇒ one half.

fr-02.statement: What part of the circle is colored?
hints: Count the equal parts.
solution: The circle has 4 equal parts and one is colored ⇒ one quarter.

hints: Divide into 2 equal parts.

fr-04.statement: What is a quarter of 20 lei?
hints: A quarter = one of 4 equal parts.

fr-05.statement: How many quarters does a whole have?
hints: A quarter is one of how many equal parts?
solution: The whole is divided into 4 equal parts ⇒ 4 quarters.

fr-06.statement: Two halves of a pizza put together make:
hints: How many halves does a whole have?
solution: A whole has 2 halves ⇒ two halves make a whole pizza.

fr-07.statement: What fraction of the strip is colored?
hints: The denominator = how many equal parts the strip is divided into; the numerator = how many parts are colored.
solution: The strip has 5 equal parts, and 3 are colored ⇒ 3/5.

fr-08.statement: In the fraction 4/7, what is the numerator?
hints: The numerator is written above the fraction bar.
solution: 4/7: the numerator is 4, the denominator is 7.

fr-09.statement: A whole is divided into 8 equal parts and we take 3 of them. What number do we write as the denominator?
hints: The denominator shows how many equal parts we divided the whole into.
solution: The whole has 8 equal parts ⇒ the denominator is 8 (the fraction is 3/8).

options: 9 parts of a whole divided into 2 equal parts
2 parts of a whole divided into 9 equal parts
hints: Read the denominator first.
solution: Denominator 9: the whole has 9 equal parts; numerator 2: we take 2 of them.
Answer: 2 parts of a whole divided into 9 equal parts.

fr-11.statement: What fraction of the circle is NOT colored?
hints: Count the white parts.
solution: The circle has 6 equal parts; 5 are colored, so 1 is not ⇒ 1/6.

fr-12.statement: What fraction of the strip is colored?
hints: How many parts does the strip have, and how many are colored?

fr-13.statement: Which fraction is equal to one whole?
hints: The numerator is equal to the denominator.
solution: 7/7: we take all 7 parts ⇒ one whole.

fr-14.statement: Which fraction is greater than one whole?
hints: The numerator is greater than the denominator.
solution: 9/4: we have 9 quarters, which is more than 4 quarters (one whole).

hints: Compare the numerator with the denominator.
solution: 5 is less than 8 ⇒ 5/8 is less than one whole: less than one whole.

fr-16.statement: What is the largest natural number □ for which the fraction □/6 is less than one whole?
hints: Less than one whole: the numerator is smaller than the denominator.
solution: □ must be less than 6 ⇒ the largest is 5 (5/6).

fr-17.statement: How many fractions less than one whole have the denominator 5 and a numerator other than 0?
hints: The numerator can be 1, 2, …
All the parts of the whole.
solution: 9/9 means all 9 parts ⇒ one whole, that is 1.

fr-19.statement: What fraction does the arrow show on the number line?
hints: Between 0 and 1 there are 4 equal steps.
solution: The unit is divided into 4 steps; the arrow is at step 3 ⇒ 3/4.

fr-20.statement: What fraction does the arrow point to on the number line?
hints: Into how many equal steps is the unit divided?
solution: The unit has 5 steps; the arrow is at step 2 ⇒ 2/5.

fr-21.statement: What fraction does the arrow show?
hints: Each unit has 2 halves; count the halves from 0.
solution: From 0, the arrow is after 3 halves ⇒ 3/2 (greater than 1).

fr-22.statement: On the number line, between 0 and 1 there are 8 equal steps. How many steps do you take from 0 to reach 5/8?
hints: Each step is 1/8.

fr-23.statement: On the number line, which fraction is closest to 1?
hints: How many more steps of 1/8 are needed to reach 1?
solution: To reach 1 = 8/8, 7/8 needs only one more step ⇒ 7/8 is the closest.

fr-24.statement: The two strips have the same colored part. Which fraction is equal to 1/2?
hints: Compare the colored part of the two strips.
solution: Half of the strip = 2 quarters of the strip ⇒ 1/2 = 2/4.

hints: How many sixths are in one half?
The denominator was multiplied by 3; do the same to the numerator.
The numerator was divided by 2; do the same to the denominator.

fr-28.statement: Of the fractions 3/5, 2/4, 4/8, 5/10 and 3/6, how many are equal to 1/2?
hints: In a half, the denominator is double the numerator.
solution: 2/4, 4/8, 5/10 and 3/6 are halves (the denominator is double the numerator); in 3/5, 5 is not double 3 ⇒ 4 fractions.

hints: What was the denominator multiplied by?
A whole divided into fewer parts has bigger parts.
solution: One third is greater than one fifth ⇒ 1/3.

hints: Same numerator: compare the size of the parts.

fr-32.statement: From two pizzas of the same size, Ana ate 2/5 of the first one and Mihai ate 2/3 of the second one. Who ate more?
hints: Both ate 2 pieces; whose pieces are bigger?
solution: Thirds are bigger than fifths ⇒ 2/3 > 2/5: Mihai ate more.

fr-33.statement: Which is the smallest of the fractions 5/6, 5/9 and 5/7?
hints: Same numerator: the largest denominator gives the smallest parts.
solution: 9 is the largest denominator ⇒ 5/9 is the smallest.

fr-34.statement: What is the smallest natural number □ for which 4/□ is less than 4/9?
hints: For a smaller fraction, the denominator must be larger.
solution: The fraction 4/□ is less than 4/9 when □ is greater than 9 ⇒ the smallest □ is 10.

fr-35.statement: What is 2/7 + 3/7? (write the numerator of the result, without simplifying)
hints: Same denominator: you add the numerators.

fr-36.statement: What is 3/10 + 4/10? (write the numerator of the result, without simplifying)
hints: The denominator stays 10.

fr-37.statement: What is 1/8 + 3/8 + 2/8? (write the numerator of the result, without simplifying)
hints: Add all the numerators.
The denominators are not added.

fr-39.statement: On Monday a pupil reads 3/8 of a book and on Tuesday another 2/8. What part of the book has he read in total? (write the numerator of the result, without simplifying)
hints: Add the parts read.

fr-40.statement: What is 7/9 − 4/9? (write the numerator of the result, without simplifying)
hints: Same denominator: you subtract the numerators.

fr-41.statement: What is 5/6 − 1/6? (write the numerator of the result, without simplifying)
hints: The denominator stays 6.
The denominators are not subtracted.

fr-43.statement: 3/8 of a cake has been eaten. What part of the cake is left? (write the numerator of the result, without simplifying)
hints: The whole cake is 8/8.
Write the whole as 5/5.

fr-45.statement: A square is divided into 4 equal parts and one part is colored. How many quarters are NOT colored?
hints: The whole has 4 quarters.
The whole has 3 thirds.

fr-47.statement: What fraction does 3/7 still need to make one whole? (write the numerator of the result, without simplifying)
hints: One whole means 7/7.

fr-48.statement: Ana has read 3/10 of a book. What part of the book does she still have to read? (write the numerator of the result, without simplifying)
hints: The whole book means 10/10.

fr-50.statement: A quarter of a number is 6. What is the number?
hints: The whole has 4 quarters.

fr-51.statement: 3/5 of a sum of money is 30 lei. How many lei is the whole sum?
hints: First find what 1/5 is.
solution: 1/5 of the sum: 30 ÷ 3 = 10 lei; the whole sum (5/5): 10 × 5 = 50 lei.

fr-52.statement: Ana has read 2/7 of a book, that is 40 pages. How many pages does the book have?
hints: What is 1/7 of the book?
solution: 1/7 of the book: 40 ÷ 2 = 20 pages; the whole book: 20 × 7 = 140 pages.

fr-53.statement: Half of a number is 35. What is the number?
hints: The whole has 2 halves.

fr-54.statement: One third of the pupils in a class is 9 pupils. How many pupils does the class have?
hints: The whole class has 3 thirds.

fr-55.statement: The square has 100 equal small squares. What fraction of it is colored? (write the numerator; the denominator is 100)
hints: Count the full rows of 10, then the rest.
solution: 3 full rows mean 30 small squares, plus 7 more ⇒ 37 small squares out of 100 ⇒ 37/100.

fr-56.statement: On a grid of 100 small squares we color a quarter of it. How many small squares do we color?
hints: A quarter of 100.
One tenth has 10 hundredths.
50 is half of 100.
solution: 50 small squares out of 100 means half ⇒ 50/100 = 1/2.

fr-59.statement: How many hundredths does 64/100 still need to make one whole?
hints: One whole has 100 hundredths.

vn-001.statement: What is the greatest two-digit natural number?
hints: Put the greatest digit in both the tens and the ones place.
solution: The greatest digit is 9, so the number is 99. After it comes 100, which has three digits.

vn-002.statement: Write the number in digits: nine thousand nine.
hints: Where the hundreds and tens are missing, you put 0.
solution: 9 thousands, no hundreds, no tens and 9 ones ⇒ 9009.

vn-003.statement: Write the number in digits: one million.
hints: One million means a thousand thousands.
solution: One million is written with 1 followed by six zeros: 1,000,000.

vn-004.statement: In a line, Maria has 3 children in front of her and 4 children behind her. How many children are in the line?
hints: Don't forget Maria.
solution: The ones in front, Maria, and the ones behind: 3 + 1 + 4 = 8.

vn-005.statement: In a race, Dan finished in place number 5, and after him 7 more children finished. How many children ran?
hints: If Dan finished in place number 5, how many finished before him?
solution: 4 children finished before Dan. In total: 4 + 1 + 7 = 12.

vn-006.statement: How many whole tens are in the number 350?
hints: One hundred has 10 tens.
solution: 3 hundreds is 30 tens, and we add the 5 tens: 30 + 5 = 35.
Careful: the tens digit is 5, but the number contains 35 tens.

vn-007.statement: What is the greatest natural number with five different digits?
hints: Put the greatest digits first, without repeating any.
solution: The five greatest different digits, in descending order: 9, 8, 7, 6, 5 ⇒ 98,765.

vn-008.statement: Which number has 0 as its ones digit?
hints: The ones digit is the last digit.
solution: 40 has 4 tens and 0 ones. The other numbers end in 4 or 1.

vn-009.statement: How many times is the digit 0 used to write the number “one thousand”?
hints: Write the number in digits.
solution: One thousand is written 1000: the digit 1 once and the digit 0 three times.

vn-010.statement: Subtract 1 from 1000. How many times does the digit 0 appear in the result?
hints: First calculate 1000 − 1.
solution: 1000 − 1 = 999. The number 999 does not contain the digit 0.

hints: It is the successor of 49.
solution: After 49 comes 50, and after 50 comes 51. The number we are looking for is 50.

vn-012.statement: The number 80 is the successor of a number. What is that number?
hints: Look for the number before 80.
solution: The successor of a number is 1 greater, so the number we are looking for is 80 − 1 = 79.

vn-013.statement: How many natural numbers are greater than 37 and less than 42?
hints: Write them all down. 37 and 42 are not counted.
solution: The numbers are 38, 39, 40 and 41, which makes 4 numbers.

vn-014.statement: Put the numbers 305, 350, 503, 530 in descending order. Which number is in third place?
hints: Descending means from the greatest to the least.
solution: In descending order: 530, 503, 350, 305. In third place is 350.

hints: Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.
solution: 0 is an even number: it ends in 0 and divides exactly by 2 (0 ÷ 2 = 0).

vn-016.statement: The sum of an even number and an odd number is always:
solution: An even number and an odd one always give an odd sum.

hints: Look at how much it grows each time: by 1, by 2, by 3…
solution: The increases are 1, 2, 3, 4, so next comes an increase by 5: 11 + 5 = 16.

hints: Each number is double the one before it.

vn-019.statement: Round the number 65 to the nearest ten.
hints: When the ones digit is 5, you round up.
solution: 65 is halfway between 60 and 70. When the ones digit is 5 or more, we round up: 70.

vn-020.statement: Round the number 96 to the nearest ten.
hints: The next ten after 90 is one hundred.
solution: 96 is between 90 and 100. The ones digit is 6, so we round up: 100.

vn-021.statement: Round the number 7950 to the nearest hundred.
hints: Look at the tens digit.
solution: 7950 is between 7900 and 8000. The tens digit is 5, so we round up: 8000.

vn-022.statement: What number is written in Roman numerals: XIX?
hints: X = 10, and IX = 9.
A symbol is not written four times in a row.
solution: The number 4 is written IV (1 less than 5), not IIII.
The others are correct: VI is 6, XI is 11, and IV is 4.

vn-024.statement: What number is written in Roman numerals: XC?
hints: C = 100, and X written before C is subtracted.
Compare the tens first.
solution: 19 has 1 ten, and 91 has 9 tens, so 19 is less than 91.
The same digits, arranged differently, give a different number.

vn-026.statement: Which number is greater than 399 and less than 401?
hints: There is only one number between them.
solution: After 399 comes 400, and after 400 comes 401. The number is 400.

hints: Count the digits of each number.
solution: 999 has three digits, and 1009 has four digits. The number with fewer digits is less: 999.

hints: Count the digits of each number.
solution: 100,000 has six digits, and 99,999 has five digits. The number with more digits is greater: 100,000.

vf-001.statement: How many halves does a whole have?
hints: A half is one of the two equal parts.

vf-002.statement: How many quarters together make a half?
hints: A whole has 4 quarters, and the half is one part out of two.
solution: The whole has 4 quarters, so the half has 4 ÷ 2 = 2 quarters.

vf-003.statement: An apple is cut into two pieces that are not equal. Is each piece a half?
options: yes: any piece is a half
only the bigger piece is a half
hints: Think about what “half” means.
solution: A half is one of two equal parts. If the pieces are not equal, neither one is a half.
Answer: no: halves must be equal.

vf-004.statement: In the fraction 5/9, what is the denominator?
hints: The denominator is the number below the fraction bar.
solution: The denominator is 9: it shows how many equal parts the whole is divided into.

vf-005.statement: A cake is cut into 6 equal slices and all the slices are eaten. What fraction of the cake was eaten?
hints: The denominator shows how many slices the cake has, and the numerator shows how many were eaten.
solution: The cake has 6 slices and 6 were eaten: the fraction is 6/6, which is the whole cake.

vf-006.statement: A chocolate bar has 10 equal squares. You eat none. What numerator does the fraction showing how much you ate have?
hints: The numerator shows how many parts you took.
solution: You took no part, so the fraction is 0/10, and the numerator is 0.

hints: Compare the numerator with the denominator.
solution: The numerator is equal to the denominator, so the fraction is equal to one whole: 9/9 = 1.

vf-008.statement: Which fraction is less than one whole (smaller than a whole)?
hints: For a fraction less than one whole, the numerator is less than the denominator.
solution: In 3/8, the numerator 3 is less than the denominator 8, so the fraction is less than one whole.
8/3 and 9/8 are greater than one whole, and 8/8 is equal to one whole.

vf-009.statement: What is the least natural number □ for which the fraction □/4 is greater than one whole?
hints: The numerator must be greater than the denominator.
solution: For □ = 4 the fraction is equal to one whole: 4/4 = 1. The first number greater than 4 is 5, so □ = 5.

vf-010.statement: On the number line, between 0 and 1 there are 4 equal steps. You start at 0 and take 4 steps toward 1. Where do you end up?
hints: Each step is a quarter.
solution: Each step is 1/4. After 4 steps you reach 4/4, which is 1.

vf-011.statement: On the number line, which fraction is exactly halfway between 0 and 1?
hints: The midpoint divides the segment into two equal parts.
solution: The midpoint of the segment between 0 and 1 is at one half: 1/2.

vf-012.statement: On the number line, which fraction is to the right of 1?
hints: To the right of 1 are the fractions greater than one whole.
solution: 7/5 is greater than one whole (7 is greater than 5), so it is to the right of 1.
5/5 is exactly 1, and 5/7 and 1/5 are between 0 and 1.

vf-013.statement: A chocolate bar has 8 equal squares. Ana eats half of the chocolate. How many squares does she eat?
hints: Divide the squares into two equal parts.
solution: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 squares. Half of the chocolate is the same as 4 squares out of 8.

vf-014.statement: Two quarters of a pizza are the same as:
hints: A pizza has 4 quarters.
solution: Two quarters out of four means half of the pizza: 2/4 and 1/2 show the same part.

hints: The more parts you divide the whole into, the smaller one part is.
solution: One tenth is much less than one half: 1/10 is less than 1/2.

vf-016.statement: A chocolate bar is shared equally among children. When does each child get a bigger piece?
options: the piece is always the same
hints: Compare 1/2, 1/4 and 1/8.
solution: The fewer children there are, the bigger the piece: 1/2 is greater than 1/4 and than 1/8.

vf-017.statement: What is the greatest natural number □ for which the fraction 3/□ is greater than 3/5?
hints: With the same numerator, the fraction is greater when the denominator is less.
solution: 3/□ is greater than 3/5 when □ is less than 5. The greatest such number is 4.

vf-018.statement: What is 3/8 + 5/8? Write the result as a natural number.
hints: Add the numerators and see what fraction you get.

vf-019.statement: What is 4/9 + 0/9? (write the numerator of the result)
hints: 0/9 means no part.
solution: 4/9 + 0/9 = 4/9: if you add nothing, the fraction stays the same.

vf-020.statement: Mihai calculated 1/5 + 2/5 and got 3/10. What did he do wrong?
hints: The parts are still fifths after the addition.
solution: Correct: 1/5 + 2/5 = 3/5. The denominator stays 5, because we add fifths to fifths; only the numerators are added.
Answer: he also added the denominators.

vf-021.statement: What is 5/7 − 5/7? Write the result as a natural number.
hints: You subtract the fraction from itself.

vf-022.statement: What is 9/9 − 4/9? (write the numerator of the result)
hints: Subtract the numerators; the denominator stays 9.
solution: 9/9 − 4/9 = 5/9. Since 9/9 is a whole, this also means 1 − 4/9 = 5/9.

hints: Subtract the numerators in each option.

vf-024.statement: A pizza has 8 equal slices and all 8 slices were eaten. How many eighths are left?
hints: 8 eighths means the whole pizza.
solution: 8/8 was eaten, which is the whole pizza. No eighth is left: 0.

vf-025.statement: How many more fifths does 1/5 need to make a whole?
hints: A whole has 5 fifths.
What is 5/5?
solution: 5/5 is already a whole, so nothing more is needed: the missing fraction is 0/5.

vf-027.statement: One tenth of a number is 10. What is the number?
hints: The whole number has 10 tenths.
solution: If one tenth is 10, then the number is 10 × 10 = 100.

vf-028.statement: 2/3 of a road is 12 km. How many kilometers is the whole road?
hints: First find how much one third is.
solution: One third of the road: 12 ÷ 2 = 6. The whole road has three thirds: 6 × 3 = 18.

vf-029.statement: 3/4 of a tank is 60 liters. How many liters fit in the whole tank?
hints: First find how much one quarter is.
solution: One quarter of the tank: 60 ÷ 3 = 20. The whole tank has four quarters: 20 × 4 = 80.

vf-030.statement: On a grid of 100 small squares we color one tenth of it. How many small squares do we color?
hints: One tenth means one of 10 equal parts.
solution: 100 ÷ 10 = 10 squares. One tenth of the grid is the same as 10/100.

vf-031.statement: On a grid of 100 small squares, 9 squares are colored. How many squares are NOT colored?
hints: Subtract from 100.
solution: 100 − 9 = 91 squares, which is 91/100 of the grid.

vf-032.statement: On a grid of 100 small squares we color all the squares. What numerator does the fraction with denominator 100 that shows the colored part have?
hints: How many squares are colored?
solution: 100 squares out of 100 are colored: the fraction is 100/100, which is the whole.

vf-033.statement: Which fraction is the least: 5/8, 1/8 or 7/8?
hints: The parts are equally big (eighths). Where are there the fewest?
solution: With the same denominator, the least fraction has the least numerator: 1/8.

vf-034.statement: What is the greatest natural number □ for which the fraction □/9 is less than 5/9?
hints: With the same denominator, you compare the numerators.
solution: □/9 is less than 5/9 when □ is less than 5. The greatest such number is 4.

vf-035.statement: How much is 1/7 of a week, in days?
hints: A week has 7 days.
solution: 7 ÷ 7 = 1: one seventh of a week is one day.

hints: 5/5 is a whole.
solution: 35 ÷ 5 = 7, then 7 × 5 = 35. Five fifths means the whole number.

hints: First find one third.

c1-mas-01.statement:
What time does the clock show?
The small hand (yellow) shows the hour, and the big hand (blue) is on the 12.
hints: Look at where the small hand (the short one) is pointing.
solution: The small hand points to 6 and the big hand is on the 12, so it is exactly 6 o'clock.

c1-mas-02.statement:
What time does the clock show?
The small hand (yellow) shows the hour, and the big hand (blue) is on the 12.
hints: Look at where the small hand (the short one) is pointing.
solution: The small hand points to 7 and the big hand is on the 12, so it is exactly 7 o'clock.

c1-mas-03.statement:
What time does the clock show?
The small hand (yellow) shows the hour, and the big hand (blue) is on the 12.
hints: Look at where the small hand (the short one) is pointing.
solution: The small hand points to 9 and the big hand is on the 12, so it is exactly 9 o'clock.

c1-mas-04.statement:
What time does the clock show?
The small hand (yellow) shows the hour, and the big hand (blue) is on the 12.
hints: Look at where the small hand (the short one) is pointing.
solution: The small hand points to 1 and the big hand is on the 12, so it is exactly 1 o'clock.

c1-mas-05.statement:
What time does the clock show?
The small hand (yellow) shows the hour, and the big hand (blue) is on the 12.
hints: Look at where the small hand (the short one) is pointing.
solution: The small hand points to 11 and the big hand is on the 12, so it is exactly 11 o'clock.

c1-mas-06.statement: You have a 5-lei bill and a 1-leu bill. How many lei do you have in total?
hints: First add up the 5-lei bills, then the 1-leu bills.

c1-mas-07.statement: You have 2 bills of 5 lei and 2 bills of 1 leu. How many lei do you have in total?
hints: First add up the 5-lei bills, then the 1-leu bills.

c1-mas-08.statement: You have 2 bills of 5 lei and 3 bills of 1 leu. How many lei do you have in total?
hints: First add up the 5-lei bills, then the 1-leu bills.

c1-mas-09.statement: You have one bill of 5 lei and 4 bills of 1 leu. How many lei do you have in total?
hints: First add up the 5-lei bills, then the 1-leu bills.

c1-mas-10.statement: Today is Wednesday. What day will it be tomorrow?
hints: Say the days of the week in order, starting with Monday.

c1-mas-11.statement: Today is Thursday. What day was it yesterday?
hints: Yesterday is the day before today.
solution: The day before Thursday is Wednesday.

c1-mas-12.statement: How many days are there in a week?

pg-01.statement: A rectangle has a length of 10 cm and a width of 7 cm. What is its perimeter?

hints: Area of a rectangle = length × width.

hints: Area of a rectangle = length × width.

pg-07.statement: A rectangle has a length of 14 cm and a width of 7 cm. What is its perimeter?

pg-19.statement: A rectangle has a length of 27 cm, and its width is 5 cm less than its length. What is the perimeter?

c1-geo-09.statement: How many circles can you see in the picture?
